01_Representing_and_naming_carbon_compou.title: Representing and naming carbon compounds
01_Representing_and_naming_carbon_compou.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Draw the displayed formula of a carbon compound showing every atom and every bond, classify it as saturated or unsaturated, and name and draw methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol.

Explain why members of a homologous series share a general formula and similar chemistry, and draw and name the unbranched alkanes and alkenes from one to four carbons, including the two different positions of the double bond in but-1-ene and but-2-ene.

prerequisites.statement: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms; carbon almost always forms exactly four covalent bonds.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every displayed formula in this lesson is built by giving each carbon exactly four bonds; without this rule a learner cannot check or draw a structure correctly.

prerequisites.statement: A molecular formula (such as C2H6) states how many atoms of each element are in one molecule, but says nothing about how those atoms are connected.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson's central idea is that the same molecular formula can hide different arrangements of bonds, which the displayed formula reveals.

diagnostic_items.question: A student draws a carbon atom in a structure with three lines coming off it (one to another carbon, two to hydrogens). Is this carbon atom's structure complete?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. Carbon must have exactly four bonds; this carbon is missing one bond, so a fourth line (to another hydrogen, in this case) must be added.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because it already has three bonds and that seems like enough.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has not internalised that carbon's bond count is fixed at four, not 'at least one' or 'a few'.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner treats four bonds as a non-negotiable rule for every carbon in every structure, not a rough guide.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner count the lines touching every single carbon in a finished diagram before moving on, circling any carbon that does not reach four.

theory_blocks.title: Why chemists draw every bond
theory_blocks.body:
Two molecules can share exactly the same molecular formula and still behave completely differently, because a molecular formula only counts atoms; it says nothing about how they are joined.

To know what a carbon compound actually is, a chemist draws its **displayed formula**: every atom shown as its symbol, and every covalent bond shown as a line between the two atoms it joins.

This matters immediately for carbon, because carbon keeps to one rule with almost no exceptions at this level: [[blue:**every carbon atom forms exactly four covalent bonds.**]] A displayed formula is really a way of checking that rule,

atom by atom, across a whole molecule at once.

theory_blocks.title: Displayed formulas of methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol
theory_blocks.body:
- **Methane**, $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$: one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. All four of carbon's bonds are used on hydrogen, so methane is the simplest possible carbon compound.
- **Ethane**, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$: two carbon atoms joined by a single C-C bond; each carbon uses its three remaining bonds on hydrogen (3 + 3 = 6 hydrogens total).
- **Ethene**, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}$: two carbon atoms joined by a **double** C=C bond (two shared electron pairs, drawn as two parallel lines); each carbon now has only two bonds left over for hydrogen (2 + 2 = 4 hydrogens total).
- **Ethanol**, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH}$: an ethane-like carbon skeleton, but one hydrogen on the second carbon is replaced by an $-\mathrm{OH}$ (hydroxyl) group; oxygen forms two bonds, one to that carbon and one to the final hydrogen.

A compound with only single C-C bonds, like methane or ethane, is called **saturated**: every carbon already carries as many hydrogens (or other atoms) as it possibly can.

A compound containing at least one C=C double bond, like ethene, is **unsaturated**: each double-bonded carbon could, in principle, accept one more atom if that double bond were opened up, which is exactly what the next lessons use.

assets.caption: Displayed formulas of methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol. Every bond carbon forms is drawn explicitly; counting the lines at any carbon atom always gives four.
assets.purpose: Lets a learner verify carbon's four-bond rule atom by atom on the four Core structures, and shows the double bond in ethene alongside single bonds elsewhere.

theory_blocks.title: Suffixes read off the family instantly
theory_blocks.body:
The ending of a compound's name announces its family before a single bond is drawn: **-ane** means saturated (single bonds only, an alkane), **-ene** means at least one C=C double bond is present (an alkene), and **-ol** means an $-\mathrm{OH}$ group is present (an alcohol).

The first part of the name (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) states the number of carbon atoms in the chain: one, two, three and four respectively.

Reading a name such as 'but-2-ene' therefore gives the whole structure before drawing anything: four carbons (but-), a double bond (-ene) that starts at the second carbon (-2-).

theory_blocks.title: A four-step method for any displayed formula
theory_blocks.body:
1. Read the name for the number of carbons (first part) and the family (suffix).
2. Draw that many carbon atoms in a row, joined by single bonds, except where the name states a double-bond position.
3. If the name is an alcohol, replace one hydrogen on the stated carbon with $-\mathrm{OH}$.
4. Fill every remaining bond on every carbon with hydrogen atoms, then check each carbon has exactly four bonds in total before calling the structure finished.

theory_blocks.title: Homologous series: alkanes and alkenes to four carbons
theory_blocks.body:
The alkanes methane, ethane, propane and butane, and the alkenes ethene, propene, but-1-ene and but-2-ene, are two **homologous series**: each is a family of compounds that (i) share one general formula,

(ii) differ from the next member only by one extra $-\mathrm{CH_{2}}-$ unit in the chain, and (iii) show a gradual, predictable change in physical properties (such as boiling point) along the series,

while showing essentially the same chemical reactions.

- Alkanes follow the general formula $\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$: methane $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ ($n=1$), ethane $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$ ($n=2$), propane $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$ ($n=3$), butane $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}$ ($n=4$).
- Alkenes follow the general formula $\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}$, starting at $n=2$ (one carbon cannot form a C=C bond with itself): ethene $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}$, propene $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}$, and but-1-ene/but-2-ene, both $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$.

From butene onward, the double bond can sit in more than one position along the chain, which is exactly why but-1-ene and but-2-ene both exist as distinct compounds with the same

molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$ but different displayed formulas (cis/trans arrangements of these are not required at this level).

assets.caption: Displayed formulas of propane and butane (alkanes, single bonds only) and of but-1-ene and but-2-ene (alkenes, same molecular formula C4H8 but the C=C double bond in a different position).
assets.purpose: Shows the Supplement-level homologous series members and makes the but-1-ene/but-2-ene distinction visible bond by bond, targeting the misconception that they are the same molecule.

keywords.definition: A diagram showing every atom in a molecule and every covalent bond between them as an explicit line.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds, so every carbon already carries the maximum number of other atoms it can hold.
Containing one or more carbon-carbon bonds that are not single bonds, such as a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
A family of compounds with the same general formula, differing by one CH2 unit between neighbouring members, and showing a gradual trend in physical properties with similar chemical reactions.
A compound containing a carbon chain with a hydroxyl (-OH) group attached, named with the suffix -ol.

worked_examples.statement: **Drawing ethane.** Draw the displayed formula of ethane, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$, and check every carbon has four bonds.
worked_examples.solution:
- Draw two carbon atoms joined by a single bond: C-C.
- Carbon 1 already has one bond (to carbon 2), so it needs three more: add three hydrogens.
- Carbon 2 is in the same position by symmetry: add three more hydrogens to it too.
- Count bonds at each carbon: carbon 1 has 1 (to C) + 3 (to H) = 4; carbon 2 has 1 (to C) + 3 (to H) = 4. Total hydrogens used: 6, matching $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The four-bond check at the end is not optional: it is how a chemist confirms a displayed formula is finished, not just plausible-looking.

worked_examples.statement: **Saturated or unsaturated?** A displayed formula shows two carbons joined by two parallel lines, with two hydrogens on each carbon. State the molecule's name, molecular formula, and whether it is saturated or unsaturated.
worked_examples.solution:
- Two parallel lines between the carbons means a C=C double bond, not two separate single bonds.
- Each carbon has: 2 (double bond, counted as one connection worth two bonds) + 2 (hydrogen) = 4 bonds, so the structure is valid.
- Two carbons with a double bond and 2+2 = 4 hydrogens gives molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}$, which is ethene.
- A C=C bond is present, so the molecule is unsaturated.
worked_examples.interpretation: Naming and classifying both come from the same two observations: how many carbons, and what kind of bond joins them.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Counting the double bond as if it used only one of carbon's four bonds, which would wrongly leave a spare bond unaccounted for.

worked_examples.statement: **But-1-ene versus but-2-ene.** Draw the displayed formulas of but-1-ene and but-2-ene, and explain, using the drawings, why a student who says 'they're both just C4H8, so they must be the same thing' is wrong.
worked_examples.solution:
- But-1-ene: number the carbons 1-2-3-4; the double bond is between carbons 1 and 2. Carbon 1 (end of chain, double-bonded) carries 2 H; carbon 2 (double-bonded, also single-bonded to carbon 3) carries 1 H; carbon 3 (both bonds single) carries 2 H; carbon 4 (end of chain, single-bonded) carries 3 H.
- But-2-ene: the double bond is between carbons 2 and 3 instead. Carbon 1 (end of chain, single-bonded) carries 3 H; carbons 2 and 3 (double-bonded to each other, single-bonded to an end carbon) each carry 1 H; carbon 4 carries 3 H.
- Adding up hydrogens in each case gives $2+1+2+3=8$ and $3+1+1+3=8$: both molecules are $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$, exactly as the student said.
- But the molecular formula only counts atoms; it cannot show where the double bond sits. The displayed formulas show that in but-1-ene carbon 4 is a full $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ group untouched by the double bond, while in but-2-ene both end carbons are $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ groups and the double bond sits in the middle. These are two different arrangements of the same atoms, so the student's reasoning (same formula implies same molecule) is incorrect.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct, worked rebuttal of the misconception that but-1-ene and but-2-ene must be the same molecule, built from counting hydrogens on each carbon rather than from memorising the two shapes.

guided_exercises.statement: Draw the displayed formula of propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$, and label each carbon with the number of hydrogens attached to it.
hints: How many carbons does 'prop-' indicate, and are they joined by single or double bonds (check the suffix)?
The two end carbons and the one middle carbon are not in the same position along the chain: will they need the same number of hydrogens?
Give every carbon exactly four bonds in total, then count how many of those are left over for hydrogen on each one.
guided_exercises.answer: Three carbons in a row, C-C-C, joined by single bonds only. The two end carbons each have one C-C bond, so each needs 3 hydrogens; the middle carbon has two C-C bonds, so it needs only 2 hydrogens. Total: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 hydrogens, matching $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$.
common_errors: Giving every carbon the same number of hydrogens (e.g. 3 each) without noticing that the middle carbon already has two C-C bonds and so has fewer bonds left for hydrogen.

guided_exercises.statement: A structural formula shows $\mathrm{CH_{3}}-\mathrm{CH_{2}}-\mathrm{OH}$. Name this compound, give its molecular formula, and state the family it belongs to.
hints: Count the carbon atoms in the chain first; which first-syllable name matches that count?
Look for a C=C double bond anywhere in the structure before deciding between -ane and -ene.
An $-\mathrm{OH}$ group attached to the chain changes the suffix to something other than -ane or -ene.
guided_exercises.answer: This is ethanol, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH}$ (molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}$): two carbons (eth-), no C=C bond, and an $-\mathrm{OH}$ group, giving the suffix -ol. It belongs to the alcohol family.
common_errors: Classifying ethanol as an alkane because it 'looks like' ethane with an extra letter, instead of noticing the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group changes the family.

exercises.statement: State, for each of methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol, whether the compound is saturated or unsaturated, giving a reason in each case.
exercises.answer: Methane: saturated, only C-H single bonds (one carbon, no C-C bond possible). Ethane: saturated, the single C-C bond and all C-H bonds are single. Ethene: unsaturated, it contains a C=C double bond. Ethanol: saturated, its carbon-carbon bond and all C-H and C-O bonds are single; the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group does not introduce a double bond.

exercises.statement: The alkane homologous series has the general formula $\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$. Use it to predict the molecular formula of pentane, the five-carbon alkane (not drawn in this lesson).
exercises.answer: General formula $\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$. For pentane, $n=5$, so $2n+2 = 12$: pentane is $\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}$.

exercises.statement: Propene, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}$, has the structure $\mathrm{CH_{2}}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$. Verify, carbon by carbon, that every carbon in this structure has exactly four bonds.
exercises.answer: Carbon 1 ($=\mathrm{CH_{2}}$): one C=C double bond (counts as 2) + 2 C-H bonds = 4. Carbon 2 ($=\mathrm{CH}-$): one C=C double bond (2) + 1 C-C single bond (1) + 1 C-H bond (1) = 4. Carbon 3 ($-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$): 1 C-C single bond + 3 C-H bonds = 4. Every carbon reaches exactly four bonds.

exercises.statement: A new unbranched alkene with five carbons, pent-2-ene, has its C=C double bond between carbons 2 and 3. Without being shown its displayed formula, predict the number of hydrogens on each of its five carbons, and its molecular formula.
exercises.answer: Carbon 1 (end, single bond only to carbon 2): 3 H. Carbon 2 (double-bonded to carbon 3, single-bonded to carbon 1): 1 H. Carbon 3 (double-bonded to carbon 2, single-bonded to carbon 4): 1 H. Carbon 4 (single bonds only, between two other carbons): 2 H. Carbon 5 (end, single bond only to carbon 4): 3 H. Total hydrogens: $3+1+1+2+3=10$, giving molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{5}H_{10}}$, consistent with the alkene general formula $\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}$ at $n=5$.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Representing and naming carbon compounds'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Representing and naming carbon compounds' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Representing and naming carbon compounds' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Draw the displayed formula of ethene. (b) State the molecular formula of ethene. (c) Explain, in terms of bonding, why ethene is described as unsaturated while ethane is described as saturated.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Two carbons joined by a C=C double bond (two parallel lines), each carbon also bonded to two hydrogen atoms. (b) $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}$. (c) Ethene contains a carbon-carbon double bond, so it is unsaturated; ethane contains only single carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds, so every carbon already carries as many hydrogens as it can hold, making it saturated.
mark_scheme: Displayed formula shows two carbons joined by a double bond, each with two hydrogens.
States molecular formula C2H4.
Identifies the C=C double bond as the reason ethene is unsaturated.
States that ethane has only single bonds, so it is saturated.

exam_questions.statement: But-1-ene and but-2-ene are both alkenes with the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$. (a) Draw the displayed formula of each. (b) Explain why two different compounds can share the same molecular formula. (c) State which carbon in but-1-ene carries three hydrogen atoms, and explain why but-2-ene has two carbons that each carry three hydrogen atoms, instead of just one.
exam_questions.answer: (a) But-1-ene: $\mathrm{CH_{2}}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH_{2}}-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$, double bond between carbons 1 and 2. But-2-ene: $\mathrm{CH_{3}}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$, double bond between carbons 2 and 3. (b) A molecular formula only records how many atoms of each element are present; it does not record which atoms are bonded to which, so different bonding arrangements (different displayed formulas) can give the same atom count. (c) Carbon 4 in but-1-ene carries three hydrogens, because it sits at the end of the chain with only a single bond to carbon 3 and no double bond. But-2-ene has two such carbons (1 and 4) because its double bond sits in the middle of the chain, between carbons 2 and 3, leaving both ends of the molecule as single-bonded $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ groups. In but-1-ene the double bond occupies one end of the chain (carbon 1), so only carbon 4 is a $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ group.
mark_scheme: Correct displayed formula of but-1-ene, double bond at position 1.
Correct displayed formula of but-2-ene, double bond at position 2.
Explains that molecular formula gives atom counts only, not bonding arrangement.
Correctly identifies carbon 4 in but-1-ene as the CH3 carbon with 3 H.
Correctly reasons that but-2-ene's central double bond leaves both end carbons as $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ groups (two carbons with 3 H each), unlike but-1-ene where the double bond occupies one end.

challenge_questions.statement: A student claims: 'but-1-ene and but-2-ene can't really be different, because you could always just flip but-1-ene's drawing over and relabel the carbons to get but-2-ene.' Decide whether flipping and relabelling but-1-ene's displayed formula can ever produce but-2-ene's displayed formula, and justify your answer by tracking where the double bond ends up.
hints: Flipping a drawing left-to-right does not move the double bond relative to the two end carbons; it only reverses which end you call 'carbon 1'.
In but-1-ene, the double bond is always attached to an end carbon; track whether that stays true after flipping and renumbering.
challenge_questions.answer: Flipping but-1-ene's displayed formula left-to-right and then renumbering from the other end does not change the double bond's position relative to the ends of the chain: it was between an end carbon and its neighbour before the flip, and it is still between an end carbon and its neighbour afterwards (just with the numbering reversed), so the flipped structure is still but-1-ene, re-drawn. In but-2-ene the double bond sits strictly between the two middle carbons, with a full $-\mathrm{CH_{3}}$ group untouched at both ends. No flip or relabelling of but-1-ene can move its double bond away from an end carbon, so the student's claim is incorrect: but-1-ene and but-2-ene are genuinely different arrangements of the same eight atoms, not the same drawing seen from two directions.
common_errors: Assuming any left-right flip of a chain can 'reach' any other arrangement, without checking what specifically stays fixed (here, the double bond's position relative to the chain ends) under that operation.

challenge_questions.statement:
The first four alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane.
(a) State the general formula for alkanes. (1 mark)
(b) Draw the displayed (full structural) formula of propane. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why alkanes are described as a 'homologous series'. (3 marks)
(d) Name and draw the structural formula of the alkane with molecular formula C₅H₁₂. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
(b) H-C-C-C-H with hydrogen atoms completing each carbon's four bonds: CH₃-CH₂-CH₃ (all C-H and C-C bonds shown explicitly).
(c) Alkanes are a homologous series because: (1) they share the same general formula (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂); (2) each successive member differs by CH₂; (3) they have similar chemical properties; (4) they show a gradual trend in physical properties (e.g. boiling point increases with chain length).
(d) Pentane: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃.

mcq.stem: Which statement about the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$ is correct?

options.text: It can only represent one possible compound.
options.why_wrong: both but-1-ene and but-2-ene share this molecular formula, so it is not unique to one compound.

options.text: It shows exactly where the double bond is in the molecule.
options.why_wrong: a molecular formula gives atom counts only; it carries no information about which atoms are bonded to which.

options.text: It is consistent with more than one displayed formula, such as but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
It proves the compound must be saturated, since the formula contains no extra information.
options.why_wrong: C4H8 actually matches the alkene general formula CnH2n, so it indicates an unsaturated compound, not a saturated one.

mcq.explanation: Both but-1-ene and but-2-ene have molecular formula C4H8; the formula alone cannot distinguish them, because it does not record bonding positions.

mcq.stem: A carbon atom in a displayed formula is shown with a double bond to one neighbouring carbon and two single bonds to hydrogen atoms. How many bonds does this carbon have in total?

options.text: 3, because the carbon is joined to three other atoms.
options.why_wrong: it is joined to three atoms, but the double bond to carbon counts as two bonds, so counting neighbouring atoms instead of bonds undercounts the double bond.

options.text: 5, because the double bond should be counted twice as a bond and then counted again as a connection.
options.why_wrong: this double-counts the double bond; it is two bonds in total between those two atoms, not two bonds plus an extra connection.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing what else is attached to the other carbon.
options.why_wrong: the bond count on this carbon only depends on what is attached to this carbon itself: one double bond (2) plus two single bonds (2) always gives 4, regardless of the far carbon's other substituents.

options.text: 4, because the double bond counts as two bonds and there are two single C-H bonds.

mcq.explanation: A C=C double bond uses two of a carbon's four bonds; adding the two C-H single bonds (2 x 1) gives 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 bonds in total, exactly satisfying carbon's valence.

mcq.stem: Which pair of compounds belongs to the same homologous series?

options.text: Ethane and propane
Methane and ethanol
options.why_wrong: methane is an alkane with only C-H bonds, while ethanol is an alcohol containing an -OH group; they differ by more than one repeating CH2 unit and do not share a general formula.

options.text: Ethene and ethanol
options.why_wrong: ethene is an unsaturated alkene (CnH2n) and ethanol is a saturated alcohol containing oxygen; they do not share a general formula.

options.text: Methane and ethene
options.why_wrong: methane is a saturated alkane and ethene is an unsaturated alkene; they belong to different series with different general formulas (CnH2n+2 versus CnH2n).

mcq.explanation: Ethane (C2H6) and propane (C3H8) are both alkanes, following the same general formula CnH2n+2 and differing by exactly one CH2 unit, the defining feature of a homologous series.

mcq.stem: Which name correctly describes the compound $\mathrm{CH_{3}}-\mathrm{CH_{2}}-\mathrm{OH}$?

options.text: Ethane
options.why_wrong: ethane, C2H6, has no oxygen and no -OH group; this structure contains an -OH group attached to a two-carbon chain.

options.text: Ethanol
Ethene
options.why_wrong: ethene contains a C=C double bond and no -OH group; this structure has only single bonds and does carry an -OH group.

options.text: Methanol
options.why_wrong: methanol has only one carbon atom; this structure has two carbon atoms in its chain.

mcq.explanation: Two carbons (eth-), no C=C bond, and a terminal -OH group give the suffix -ol: this is ethanol.

flashcards.front: What does a displayed formula show that a molecular formula does not?
flashcards.back: Every individual atom and every individual bond, including exactly which atoms are joined to which.

flashcards.front: What is the rule for how many covalent bonds a carbon atom forms?
flashcards.back: Exactly four, in almost every compound met at this level.

flashcards.front: What is the structural difference between a saturated and an unsaturated carbon compound?
flashcards.back: A saturated compound has only single C-C bonds; an unsaturated compound contains at least one C=C double bond.

flashcards.front: If but-1-ene and but-2-ene both have molecular formula C4H8, are they the same compound?
flashcards.back: No. The molecular formula only counts atoms; the two compounds have the double bond in different positions, so their displayed formulas, and therefore their identities, are different.

flashcards.front: What is the general formula of the alkane homologous series, and what is it for alkenes?
flashcards.back: Alkanes: CnH(2n+2). Alkenes: CnH(2n). (The syllabus does not require you to recall these, but you must be able to use a general formula when it is given.)

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A molecular formula such as C4H8 shows exactly where every bond in the molecule is, so it is just as informative as a displayed formula.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Molecular formulas are the first formulas learners meet, so they expect any formula to carry full structural information.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner tries to decide whether a compound is but-1-ene or but-2-ene using only the molecular formula C4H8, without asking for more information.
misconceptions.correct_model: A molecular formula only gives atom counts. Two different compounds (even a saturated and an unsaturated one, in other cases) can share a molecular formula; the displayed formula is needed to show which atoms are bonded to which.
misconceptions.remediation: Show two displayed formulas that both reduce to C4H8 (but-1-ene and but-2-ene) and ask the learner to find the molecular formula of each; both give C4H8, proving the formula alone cannot distinguish them.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A double bond (C=C) means there are two extra carbon atoms compared with a single bond (C-C).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'double' and the doubled line in the drawing suggest 'twice as much structure', which learners generalise to 'twice as many atoms'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says ethene has more carbon atoms than ethane because ethene has a double bond.
misconceptions.correct_model: A double bond is two shared pairs of electrons between the same two carbon atoms, not a bond to a different, extra atom. Ethene (C2H4) and ethane (C2H6) both have exactly two carbon atoms; only the number of hydrogens attached to those two carbons, and the kind of bond joining them, differs.
misconceptions.remediation: Place the ethane and ethene displayed formulas side by side and ask the learner to count carbon atoms only, ignoring bonds, in each; both give two carbons, however many lines join them.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: But-1-ene and but-2-ene are really the same molecule just written slightly differently, since both have four carbons and one C=C double bond.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both names look almost identical and both describe 'a butene', so learners assume the number after 'but' is a minor labelling detail rather than a real structural difference.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner cannot explain, using the displayed formulas, why but-1-ene and but-2-ene need two different names.
misconceptions.correct_model: The number states which carbon-carbon bond, counting from one end of the chain, is the double bond: between carbons 1 and 2 in but-1-ene, between carbons 2 and 3 in but-2-ene. Moving the double bond changes which carbons carry two hydrogens and which carry one, so the two displayed formulas are genuinely different arrangements of the same four carbons and eight hydrogens.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to draw both displayed formulas from scratch, number the carbons 1 to 4 in each, and state in words exactly where the double bond sits in each one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a double bond as if it only used one of carbon's four bonds.
common_mistakes.why: The double bond looks like 'one connection' to the other carbon, so learners count it as one bond rather than two.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always count a double bond as worth two bonds when checking that a carbon reaches a total of four.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming that sharing a molecular formula means two compounds must be identical.
common_mistakes.why: A molecular formula feels like a complete description, because it is the only formula many learners have used before.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether the displayed formula, not just the atom count, has been compared before concluding two compounds are the same.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving every carbon in a chain the same number of hydrogens, regardless of its position.
common_mistakes.why: It feels simpler to treat every carbon in a chain identically rather than checking each one's own bonds.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Count how many C-C or C=C bonds each individual carbon already has before deciding how many hydrogens it needs.

exam_notes: When asked to draw a displayed formula, show every atom and every bond explicitly; a skeletal or shorthand formula will not earn displayed-formula marks.
When distinguishing but-1-ene from but-2-ene, state the double bond's position using the lowest possible carbon number along the chain.

summary.big_idea: A displayed formula fixes exactly how a carbon compound's atoms are bonded, which a molecular formula alone cannot do, and the compound's name (chain length plus suffix) encodes that structure directly.

But-1-ene and but-2-ene share the molecular formula C4H8 but have the C=C double bond in different positions, making them different compounds.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Give every carbon exactly four bonds (a double bond counts as two) and the displayed formula will always be correct; the molecular formula alone can never tell you where that double bond sits.

theory_blocks.title: One liquid, many different molecules
theory_blocks.body:
Crude oil (petroleum) looks like a single thick, dark liquid, but it is a [[blue:**mixture**]] of many hundreds of different hydrocarbon compounds, mostly alkanes, with chain lengths ranging from very short (a few carbons) to very long (dozens of carbons).

Because it is a mixture, not a single compound, it does not have one fixed boiling point; instead, each hydrocarbon inside it keeps its own boiling point, and that is exactly the property fractional distillation exploits.

Natural gas, found alongside petroleum deposits, is mostly **methane**. The three **fossil fuels** are **coal, natural gas and petroleum**; they are called fossil fuels because they formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms.

theory_blocks.title: Fractional distillation: sorting by boiling range
theory_blocks.body:
Crude oil is heated until most of it vaporises and fed into the bottom of a tall **fractionating column**, which is hotter at the bottom and progressively cooler towards the top. As the vapour rises:

- Hydrocarbons with **short chains** have **low boiling points**; they stay as vapour until very near the top of the column, where it is cool enough for them to condense, and are collected there.
- Hydrocarbons with **long chains** have **high boiling points**; they condense back to liquid almost immediately, low down in the column, and are collected near the bottom.

This sorts the mixture into several **fractions**, each itself still a mixture, but one containing hydrocarbons within a narrower range of chain lengths and boiling points than crude oil as a whole.

No chemical bonds are broken: this is a physical separation, driven entirely by differences in boiling point.

[[blue:**Supplement (C11.3.7).**]] Describing the separation itself is Core. Linking the fractions to **chain length** (short chains collected high in the column, long chains low down) and explaining the boiling-point trend is Supplement material; it is developed in the ADVANCED block *Why chain length controls boiling point*.

assets.caption: A fractionating column: crude oil vapour enters at the bottom and cools as it rises, so each fraction condenses and is drawn off at the height where the column is cool enough for its boiling range. The boiling ranges shown are approximate.
assets.purpose: Shows the five required fractions in their correct top-to-bottom order, tied to approximate boiling ranges and to chain length, with the boiling-point trend outside the column outline.

theory_blocks.title: Five fractions, five uses
theory_blocks.body:
- **Refinery gas** (shortest chains, lowest boiling point): used for heating and cooking.
- **Petrol (gasoline)**: used as fuel for cars.
- **Naphtha**: used mainly as a chemical feedstock, the starting material for making many other chemicals (including, later, polymers).
- **Diesel oil**: used as fuel for diesel engines.
- **Bitumen** (longest chains, highest boiling point, drawn off as a liquid/semi-solid residue at the bottom): used for surfacing roads and roofing.

Moving down this list, chain length increases, boiling point increases, and the fractions generally become thicker (more viscous) and harder to ignite.

theory_blocks.title: Why chain length controls boiling point

keywords.definition: A fuel such as coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms.
A naturally occurring mixture of many different hydrocarbon compounds, mostly alkanes.
A physical separation process that sorts a mixture into fractions using differences in boiling point.
A group of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and a narrower boiling range, collected together in distillation.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the column.** A fraction is collected from very near the top of a fractionating column. State, with a reason, whether this fraction has short or long hydrocarbon chains, and whether its boiling point is relatively high or low.
worked_examples.solution:
- The top of the column is the coolest part.
- A fraction is only collected at a height where the column is cool enough for it to condense back to liquid.
- Condensing at the coolest part of the column means this fraction has a relatively low boiling point.
- Low boiling point corresponds to short hydrocarbon chains, so this fraction has short chains (such as refinery gas).
worked_examples.interpretation: Position in the column, boiling point and chain length always move together: reading off one tells you the other two.

worked_examples.statement: **Matching fraction to use.** A refinery technician needs a fraction suited to surfacing a road. Name the fraction and justify the choice using its position in the column.
worked_examples.solution:
- Road surfacing requires a thick, high-boiling material that will not simply run off or evaporate: this points to a fraction from near the bottom of the column.
- The fraction collected lowest in the column, with the longest chains and highest boiling point, is bitumen.
- Bitumen is exactly the fraction used for surfacing roads (and roofing), consistent with its long chains and high viscosity.
worked_examples.interpretation: Matching a use to a fraction works by reasoning from the required physical property back to chain length and column position, not by memorising an unconnected list.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining the trend.** Explain why naphtha, collected partway up the column, has a lower boiling point than diesel oil, collected further down, in terms of the molecules present.
worked_examples.solution:
- Naphtha is collected higher in the column than diesel oil, so naphtha condenses at a cooler point in the column than diesel oil does.
- A substance only condenses once the surrounding temperature drops to or below its own boiling point, so naphtha's boiling point must be lower than diesel oil's.
- Hydrocarbon chain length and boiling point increase together within this mixture, so naphtha's molecules have shorter chains, on average, than diesel oil's.
- Shorter chains mean weaker intermolecular attractions between the molecules, which take less energy to overcome, giving naphtha its lower boiling point.
worked_examples.interpretation: This threads column position, boiling point and chain length into one explanatory chain, which is exactly the Supplement-level reasoning the objective asks for.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping at 'naphtha is higher up' without connecting that position back to an actual physical reason (chain length and intermolecular attraction) for the boiling-point difference.

guided_exercises.statement: A fraction is described as 'used as fuel for cars'. Name the fraction and state its approximate position in the column (top, upper-middle, middle, lower-middle or bottom).
hints: Which of the five named fractions has 'fuel for cars' as its stated use?
Petrol is lighter and shorter-chain than diesel, naphtha or bitumen, but not as short-chain as refinery gas.
guided_exercises.answer: Petrol (gasoline); it is collected in the upper part of the column, below refinery gas but above naphtha, diesel oil and bitumen.
common_errors: Confusing petrol with diesel oil, since both are liquid transport fuels; the two are collected at different heights and have different typical uses (cars versus diesel engines).

guided_exercises.statement: Explain why heating crude oil and letting it vaporise, then cooling the vapour so it condenses again, does not create any new substances.
hints: Think about what boiling and condensing actually do to a substance's chemical bonds.
Compare this with the definition of a physical change versus a chemical change.
guided_exercises.answer: Boiling and condensing are physical changes of state: they change how closely packed and how fast-moving the molecules are, but they do not break or form any covalent bonds within those molecules. The same hydrocarbon molecules that were present in the crude oil are still present, unchanged, in whichever fraction they end up in.
common_errors: Describing distillation as a chemical reaction that 'produces' the fractions, rather than a physical sorting of substances already present.

exercises.statement: List the five named fractions of crude oil in order from the top of the fractionating column to the bottom, giving one named use for each.
exercises.answer: Top to bottom: refinery gas (heating and cooking); petrol (fuel for cars); naphtha (chemical feedstock); diesel oil (fuel for diesel engines); bitumen (surfacing roads).

exercises.statement: State whether each of the following is a physical process or a chemical reaction, giving a reason: (a) heating crude oil until it vaporises; (b) vapour condensing back to liquid at a particular height in the column.
exercises.answer: (a) Physical process: vaporising only changes the state of the hydrocarbons present (liquid to gas); no covalent bonds are broken. (b) Physical process: condensing only changes gas back to liquid; again, no covalent bonds are broken or formed.

exercises.statement: A student says: 'Naphtha must have a higher boiling point than petrol, because naphtha is collected lower down in the column.' Decide whether this reasoning is valid.
exercises.answer: The reasoning is valid: a lower collection point corresponds to a warmer part of the column, so a fraction collected there must need a higher temperature to condense, meaning it has a higher boiling point. Naphtha, collected below petrol, therefore does have a higher boiling point than petrol, consistent with the general top-to-bottom trend.

exercises.statement: A laboratory distils a mixture of two liquids, X (boiling point 60 °C) and Y (boiling point 150 °C), using a miniature fractionating column. Predict which liquid condenses and is collected first as the mixture is gently heated, and explain your reasoning using the same principle that explains crude oil's fractions.
exercises.answer: Liquid X (boiling point 60 °C) is collected first: with the lower boiling point, X vaporises and reaches a condensing temperature earlier (at a lower overall heating temperature, or higher/cooler point in a column) than Y, exactly as shorter-chain, lower-boiling fractions of crude oil are collected before longer-chain, higher-boiling fractions in the same distillation process.

exam_questions.answer: (a) A mixture of many different hydrocarbon compounds (mostly alkanes) of different chain lengths. (b) Boiling point (or boiling range). (c) For example, diesel oil, used as fuel for diesel engines (any one of the five fractions with its correct stated use is acceptable).

exam_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of chain length, intermolecular attraction and boiling point, why bitumen is collected at the bottom of a fractionating column while refinery gas is collected at the top.
exam_questions.answer: Bitumen is made of hydrocarbons with very long chains; long chains have strong intermolecular attractions between molecules, which take a great deal of energy to overcome, giving bitumen a very high boiling point, so it condenses low down (near the hot bottom) in the column and is drawn off there as a liquid/semi-solid residue. Refinery gas is made of hydrocarbons with very short chains; short chains have much weaker intermolecular attractions, giving refinery gas a very low boiling point, so it stays as vapour until it reaches the cool top of the column, where it finally condenses and is collected.
mark_scheme: States bitumen has long chains.
Links long chains to strong intermolecular attraction and high boiling point.
States refinery gas has short chains, weak intermolecular attraction, low boiling point.
Correctly links each fraction's boiling point to where in the column (hot bottom or cool top) it condenses.
Gives a scientifically coherent explanation connecting all of chain length, attraction, boiling point and column position.

challenge_questions.statement:
Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
(a) Explain why fractional distillation works, in terms of intermolecular forces and boiling points. (3 marks)
(b) Name three fractions obtained and state a use for each. (3 marks)
(c) Explain the trend in viscosity and flammability as chain length increases. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why crude oil is described as a 'finite resource' and state one alternative energy source. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths and therefore different boiling points. Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces (more surface contact between molecules) and higher boiling points. In the fractionating column, vapours rise and condense at different heights — shorter chains condense higher up (lower b.p.), longer chains condense lower down.
(b) Petrol/gasoline — vehicle fuel; kerosene — jet fuel; bitumen — road surfacing. (Also: diesel — lorries/buses; naphtha — chemical feedstock.)
(c) As chain length increases: viscosity increases (molecules tangle more) and flammability decreases (harder to vaporise due to stronger intermolecular forces).
(d) Crude oil is finite because it took millions of years to form from ancient organisms and is being used much faster than it can be replaced. Alternative: solar/wind/nuclear/hydrogen fuel cells.

options.text: It is a single pure hydrocarbon compound.
options.why_wrong: crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbon compounds, not one pure compound.

options.text: It contains no carbon-based compounds at all.
options.why_wrong: hydrocarbons, by definition, contain carbon and hydrogen; crude oil is almost entirely hydrocarbons.

options.text: It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbon compounds.
It boils completely at one single, fixed temperature.
options.why_wrong: a mixture of many different hydrocarbons does not have one single fixed boiling point; its components boil across a range of temperatures, which is exactly what fractional distillation exploits.

options.text: A chemical reaction that converts crude oil into several new compounds.
options.why_wrong: no new compounds are made; distillation is a physical separation of substances already present in the crude oil.

options.text: Crude oil is filtered through a solid material that traps longer molecules.
options.why_wrong: fractional distillation separates by boiling point difference, not by filtration through a solid.

options.text: Carbon-carbon bonds in crude oil are broken to form smaller fractions.

mcq.stem: Why does a fraction with short hydrocarbon chains condense near the top of the column rather than near the bottom?

Short chains react with the column material only near the top.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Petroleum (crude oil) is a single pure compound, not a mixture of different substances.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Crude oil looks like one uniform dark liquid, so learners assume 'one substance' rather than imagining hundreds of different hydrocarbons mixed together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner asks for 'the formula of petroleum', or expects a fixed boiling point for the whole liquid rather than a range.
misconceptions.correct_model: Petroleum is a mixture of very many different hydrocarbon compounds (mostly alkanes) of different chain lengths, each with its own boiling point; this is exactly why it can be separated into fractions by boiling range rather than boiling at one single temperature.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what a temperature–time graph looks like while a single pure compound boils (a flat section at its boiling point), then compare it with crude oil, whose temperature keeps rising gradually as different fractions boil off in turn.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Fractional distillation separates crude oil by a chemical reaction that breaks it into different products.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The idea of 'making different products from crude oil' sounds like a chemical process, and heating is strongly associated with reactions elsewhere in the course.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes the fractions as 'produced' or 'made' by the column, rather than as hydrocarbons that were already present in the crude oil and have simply been sorted by boiling range.
misconceptions.correct_model: Fractional distillation is a physical separation: it uses only differences in boiling point to sort hydrocarbon molecules that were already present in the crude oil into groups (fractions). No new substances are formed and no chemical bonds are broken in the process.
misconceptions.remediation: List the hydrocarbons present in a sample before and after distillation; show that the same molecules are simply now sorted into different collecting points, not changed into new ones.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Bitumen, because it is heavy and thick, must rise to the top of the fractionating column like everything else, or escape as a gas from the top.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes assume 'gas comes out of the top' applies to every fraction, without connecting bitumen's very high boiling point to the fact that it barely vaporises at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner places bitumen at the top of a labelled column diagram, or describes it leaving the column as a gas.
misconceptions.correct_model: Bitumen has the longest carbon chains and the highest boiling point of the named fractions; at the temperatures used, it does not vaporise and is drawn off as a liquid/semi-solid residue at the bottom of the column, not collected as a gas at the top.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace the column from bottom (hottest, longest chains, bitumen never fully vaporises) to top (coolest, shortest chains, refinery gas never condenses) and ask the learner to place all five fractions in order before naming any of them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating crude oil as if it were one pure substance with a single boiling point.
common_mistakes.why: A visually uniform liquid is assumed to be chemically uniform too.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that distillation only works at all because crude oil is a mixture; a pure compound could not be separated this way.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing fractional distillation as a chemical reaction that 'makes' the fractions.
common_mistakes.why: Heating is strongly associated with reactions elsewhere in chemistry.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether any new substance has appeared; distillation only sorts substances already present by boiling point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Placing bitumen at the top of the column, or describing it leaving as a gas.
common_mistakes.why: Learners over-generalise 'gas leaves at the top' to every fraction, without checking whether that fraction actually vaporises at the temperatures used.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check each fraction's boiling point against the column's temperature range before deciding whether it would even vaporise.

exam_notes: When asked to describe fractional distillation, mention both the direction of the temperature gradient (hot at the bottom, cool at the top) and the physical (not chemical) nature of the separation.
Learn the five named fractions with their uses as a matched pair, not as two separate lists.
An explanation of the top-to-bottom trend should mention chain length, intermolecular attraction and boiling point together, not boiling point alone.

summary.big_idea: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that fractional distillation physically sorts by boiling point, which tracks chain length, so shorter chains collect near the cool top of the column and longer chains near the hot bottom.
key_points: Crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbon compounds, mostly alkanes, not a single pure substance.
Fractional distillation is a physical process (boiling and condensing); it breaks no chemical bonds and makes no new substances.
Top to bottom: refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, diesel oil, bitumen, with chain length and boiling point both increasing down the column.
Longer chains have stronger intermolecular attractions, hence higher boiling points, which is why they condense lower in the column.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Chain length, intermolecular attraction and boiling point all increase together down the column; where a fraction condenses is simply where the column has finally cooled enough for that fraction's own boiling point.

exit_check.question: A student says bitumen must leave the column as a gas from the top, 'because that is what happens to everything eventually'. What is wrong with this reasoning?
exit_check.answer: Bitumen's very long chains give it an extremely high boiling point, far above the temperature anywhere in the column; it never fully vaporises and is instead drawn off as a liquid/semi-solid residue at the hot bottom of the column, not collected as a gas at the cool top.

objectives.statement: Describe alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons containing only single covalent bonds, state that they are generally unreactive except in combustion, and write and balance equations for the complete combustion of an alkane.

prerequisites.statement: Alkanes (methane, ethane, propane, butane) are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single C-C and C-H bonds.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson's central claim, that alkanes are generally unreactive, is explained by the strength of these single bonds; without the structure, 'unreactive' is just an unexplained label.

prerequisites.statement: A chemical equation is balanced when the same number of atoms of each element appears on both sides.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every combustion equation in this lesson must be checked atom by atom; without the balancing skill, a wrong equation can look plausible.

theory_blocks.title: Strong bonds, few reactions
theory_blocks.body:
Alkanes are [[blue:**saturated hydrocarbons**]]: every carbon-carbon bond is a single bond, and every carbon already carries as many hydrogens as its four bonds allow.

Single C-C and C-H covalent bonds are strong and need a large amount of energy to break, which is exactly why alkanes take part in very few reactions under normal conditions: there is no 'spare',

easily opened bond (like the C=C double bond met in the next lesson) for another substance to attack.

This does not mean alkanes never react. It means they are **generally unreactive**, reacting readily really only when supplied with enough energy to break their strong single bonds, which is exactly what happens when they burn.

assets.caption: Left: propane's displayed formula, every bond a single bond (saturated). Right: an atom-by-atom tally confirming methane's complete combustion equation is correctly balanced.
assets.purpose: Links the structural reason for low reactivity (all single bonds) directly beside a worked numeric check of the one reaction alkanes do undergo readily.

theory_blocks.title: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel
theory_blocks.body:
When a hydrocarbon fuel burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen, **complete combustion** occurs: every carbon atom ends up in carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, and every hydrogen atom ends up in water, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$.

In words: hydrocarbon + oxygen $\to$ carbon dioxide + water.

For methane: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \to CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$. Checking atom by atom: 1 carbon on each side; 4 hydrogens on each side ($2\times2$ on the right);

4 oxygens on each side ($2\times2$ on the left, $2+2\times1$ on the right) -- the equation is balanced.

This single reaction, repeated for every alkane, is the practical reason alkanes are used as fuels: it releases a large amount of energy as the strong bonds in the fuel and in oxygen

are replaced by the even stronger bonds in carbon dioxide and water.

theory_blocks.title: 'Unreactive' is relative, not absolute

keywords.definition: A hydrocarbon containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water from a hydrocarbon fuel.
A saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula CnH(2n+2).

worked_examples.statement: **Balancing methane combustion.** Write and balance the equation for the complete combustion of methane.
worked_examples.solution:
- Start from the word equation: methane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
- Write the formulas: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + O_{2} \to CO_{2} + H_{2}O}$.
- Balance carbon: 1 on each side already -- no change needed.
- Balance hydrogen: 4 on the left, only 2 on the right; put a 2 in front of $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + O_{2} \to CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$.
- Balance oxygen: the right now has $2 + 2 = 4$ oxygens, so the left needs 4 oxygens too; put a 2 in front of $\mathrm{O_{2}}$: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \to CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$.
- Final check: C 1=1, H 4=4, O 4=4. Balanced.
worked_examples.interpretation: Balancing hydrogen before oxygen avoids having to revisit the hydrogen count later, since water is the only product carrying hydrogen.

worked_examples.statement: **Balancing propane combustion.** Write and balance the equation for the complete combustion of propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$.
worked_examples.solution:
- Word equation: propane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
- Formulas: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + O_{2} \to CO_{2} + H_{2}O}$.
- Balance carbon: 3 carbons on the left need 3 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ on the right: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + O_{2} \to 3CO_{2} + H_{2}O}$.
- Balance hydrogen: 8 hydrogens on the left need 4 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ on the right: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + O_{2} \to 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}$.
- Balance oxygen: the right now has $3\times2 + 4\times1 = 10$ oxygens, so 5 $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ are needed on the left: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + 5O_{2} \to 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}$.
- Final check: C 3=3, H 8=8, O 10=10. Balanced.
worked_examples.interpretation: Balancing carbon and hydrogen first, then finding whatever oxygen total is needed last, works for any hydrocarbon combustion equation, not only methane.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to balance oxygen before carbon and hydrogen are both fixed, which usually forces a fraction or a second revision.

worked_examples.statement: **Why does the combustion equation for propane have a factor of 5 in front of $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, while methane only needs 2?** Explain the difference by comparing the two fuels' formulas.
worked_examples.solution:
- Methane, $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$, has 1 carbon and 4 hydrogens to account for; this needs 1 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ (2 oxygens) plus 2 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ (2 oxygens), a total of 4 oxygen atoms, or 2 $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ molecules.
- Propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$, has 3 carbons and 8 hydrogens to account for; this needs 3 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ (6 oxygens) plus 4 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ (4 oxygens), a total of 10 oxygen atoms, or 5 $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ molecules.
- Propane has more carbon and hydrogen atoms per molecule than methane, so completely combusting one propane molecule simply needs more oxygen atoms, and therefore more $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ molecules, than completely combusting one methane molecule.
worked_examples.interpretation: The oxygen coefficient is not an arbitrary number to memorise per fuel: it falls directly out of how many carbon and hydrogen atoms that fuel's own formula contains.

guided_exercises.statement: State, with a reason linked to bonding, why alkanes take part in relatively few chemical reactions compared with many other families of compounds.
hints: What kind of bond (single or double) joins the carbons in an alkane?
Is there any 'spare', easily opened bond in an alkane (like the second bond of a C=C double bond in an alkene) that another molecule could add across?
guided_exercises.answer: Alkanes contain only single C-C and C-H covalent bonds, which are strong and need a large amount of energy to break; without an easily opened bond such as a C=C double bond, there is no obvious point for another substance to attack, so alkanes undergo relatively few reactions under normal conditions.
common_errors: Stating only that alkanes 'are unreactive' without linking this to the single-bond structure that actually causes it.

guided_exercises.statement: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of butane: $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10} + O_{2} \to CO_{2} + H_{2}O}$.
hints: Balance carbon first: how many CO2 does one C4H10 molecule need?
Balance hydrogen next: how many H2O does one C4H10 molecule need?
Butane's hydrogen count is even but the oxygen total may come out odd for one butane molecule; try doubling every coefficient, including butane's own, if that happens.
guided_exercises.answer: $2\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}} + 13\mathrm{O_{2}} \to 8\mathrm{CO_{2}} + 10\mathrm{H_{2}O}$. Check: C $2\times4=8$ both sides; H $2\times10=20$ both sides ($10\times2=20$ on the right); O $13\times2=26$ on the left, $8\times2+10\times1=26$ on the right.
common_errors: Stopping at a half-integer coefficient for O2 (6.5) instead of doubling every coefficient in the equation to clear it.

exercises.statement: State the meaning of 'saturated' as it applies to alkanes, and explain why this is a different meaning from 'a saturated solution'.
exercises.answer: For alkanes, saturated means every carbon-carbon bond is a single bond, so every carbon already carries the maximum number of hydrogens its four bonds allow. This is a statement about bonding in a molecule, unrelated to a saturated solution, which describes a solvent holding the maximum amount of dissolved solute it can.

exercises.statement: Explain why 'alkanes are unreactive' is not strictly correct, and suggest a better way to phrase the statement.
exercises.answer: Alkanes do react, for example in combustion with oxygen, so 'unreactive' on its own is too strong. A better phrasing is 'alkanes are generally unreactive (relatively unreactive compared with unsaturated hydrocarbons), reacting readily mainly in combustion'.

exercises.statement: A student writes the equation for the complete combustion of methane as $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \to CO + 2H_{2}O}$. Identify the error and correct the equation.
exercises.answer: The product should be carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, not carbon monoxide, $\mathrm{CO}$, for complete combustion with a plentiful oxygen supply (the student's equation is also unbalanced: 4 oxygen atoms on the left but only 3 on the right). Corrected equation: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \to CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$, which balances: C 1=1, H 4=4, O 4=4.

exercises.statement: Ethane, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$, is used as a fuel in some industrial processes. Write and balance the equation for its complete combustion, using the same method as for methane and propane.
exercises.answer: Balance carbon: 2 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$. Balance hydrogen: 3 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ (6 hydrogens). Oxygen needed: $2\times2 + 3\times1 = 7$, an odd number, so double every coefficient: $2\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}} + 7\mathrm{O_{2}} \to 4\mathrm{CO_{2}} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O}$. Check: C $2\times2=4$ both sides; H $2\times6=12$ both sides ($6\times2=12$); O $7\times2=14$ both sides ($4\times2+6\times1=14$).

exam_questions.answer: (a) A hydrocarbon containing only single carbon-carbon bonds, so every carbon carries the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms. (b) Carbon dioxide and water.

exam_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of bonding, why alkanes are generally unreactive but do undergo combustion, and write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$.
exam_questions.answer: Alkanes contain only strong single covalent bonds (C-C and C-H), which need a large amount of energy to break, so alkanes take part in few reactions under normal conditions. Combustion is an exception because burning supplies enough energy (ignition) to break these bonds and allow the carbon and hydrogen atoms to form new, even stronger bonds with oxygen, releasing energy overall. Balanced equation: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + 5O_{2} \to 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}$.

challenge_questions.statement:
(a) Write balanced equations for the complete and incomplete combustion of propane (C₃H₈). (3 marks)
(b) Explain why incomplete combustion is dangerous and how it can be detected. (2 marks)
(c) A gas boiler produces a yellow, sooty flame instead of a blue flame. Explain what this indicates and what should be done. (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Complete: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Incomplete (forming CO): 2C₃H₈ + 7O₂ → 6CO + 8H₂O. Incomplete (forming C): C₃H₈ + 2O₂ → 3C + 4H₂O.
(b) Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (CO), which is colourless and odourless, making it hard to detect without a CO alarm. It is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport.
(c) A yellow, sooty flame indicates incomplete combustion — insufficient oxygen is reaching the burner. Soot (carbon) is being produced. The boiler should be serviced immediately to adjust the air supply, as carbon monoxide may also be produced, posing a serious health risk.

mcq.stem: What does it mean to say that an alkane is 'saturated'?

options.text: It has dissolved the maximum possible amount of another substance.
options.why_wrong: this is the meaning of a saturated solution, not a saturated hydrocarbon; the two uses of 'saturated' describe different things.

options.text: It contains the maximum possible number of carbon atoms for its boiling point.
options.why_wrong: saturation refers to bond type, not to a relationship between carbon count and boiling point.

options.text: Every carbon-carbon bond in it is a single bond.
It cannot burn in oxygen under any circumstances.
options.why_wrong: alkanes burn readily in oxygen (combustion); saturation describes their bonding, not an inability to react.

mcq.explanation: A saturated hydrocarbon, such as an alkane, contains only single carbon-carbon bonds, so every carbon already carries as many hydrogens as it can hold.

mcq.stem: Which statement best describes alkane reactivity?

options.text: Alkanes never take part in any chemical reaction.
options.why_wrong: alkanes do react, most importantly in combustion; 'unreactive' is a comparison, not an absolute statement.

options.text: Alkanes are more reactive than alkenes under all conditions.
options.why_wrong: the C=C double bond in alkenes makes them generally more reactive than the single-bonded alkanes, not less.

options.text: Alkanes only react when dissolved in water.
options.why_wrong: combustion, the key alkane reaction in this course, does not require the alkane to be dissolved in water.

options.text: Alkanes are generally unreactive, but burn readily in oxygen (combustion).

mcq.explanation: Alkanes' strong single bonds make them generally unreactive, but they do react readily with oxygen in combustion, which is the key reaction covered at this level.

mcq.stem: What are the two products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
Carbon monoxide and water
options.why_wrong: carbon monoxide is a product of incomplete combustion (limited oxygen); complete combustion, with plentiful oxygen, produces carbon dioxide instead.

options.text: Carbon and hydrogen gas
options.why_wrong: combustion does not leave carbon or hydrogen as uncombined elements when oxygen is plentiful; both end up combined with oxygen, as CO2 and H2O.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.why_wrong: the hydrogen in the fuel ends up combined with oxygen as water, not released as uncombined hydrogen gas.

mcq.explanation: Complete combustion, with a plentiful oxygen supply, converts every carbon atom in the fuel to carbon dioxide and every hydrogen atom to water.

mcq.stem: Which coefficient correctly balances $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}} + \_\,\mathrm{O_{2}} \to 3\mathrm{CO_{2}} + 4\mathrm{H_{2}O}$?

options.text: 3, matching the number of carbons.
options.why_wrong: the oxygen coefficient must balance total oxygen atoms on both sides (6 from CO2 plus 4 from H2O = 10), not simply copy the carbon count.

options.text: 4, matching the number of water molecules.
options.why_wrong: 4 O2 would supply only 8 oxygen atoms, short of the 10 oxygen atoms needed by the products shown.

options.text: 8, matching the number of hydrogens in propane.
options.why_wrong: 8 O2 would supply 16 oxygen atoms, far more than the 10 actually needed; the hydrogen count in propane is not the quantity being balanced here.

mcq.explanation: The products contain $3\times2 + 4\times1 = 10$ oxygen atoms, which requires 5 $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ molecules (5x2 = 10) on the reactant side.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: 'Saturated', as used for alkanes, means the same thing as a saturated solution: as much solute as a solvent can possibly dissolve.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners meet 'saturated solution' earlier in the course, and the everyday meaning of 'saturated' as 'completely full' transfers across without checking the actual definition in this new context.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner tries to explain why an alkane is saturated using dissolving or solubility language.
misconceptions.correct_model: In organic chemistry, 'saturated' describes bonding, not dissolving: a saturated hydrocarbon contains only single C-C bonds, so every carbon already carries as many hydrogens (or other atoms) as its four bonds allow. The word is unrelated to how much of something can dissolve in a solvent.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to state the definition of 'saturated' they are using, then compare it directly with the single-bonds-only definition, side by side, for the two different contexts.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Alkanes can never react under any circumstances, since they are described as 'unreactive'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Unreactive' is read as an absolute, all-or-nothing statement rather than as a comparison (relatively unreactive compared with, for example, alkenes).
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims an alkane cannot burn, or cannot react with anything at all, when asked about combustion.
misconceptions.correct_model: Alkanes are described as 'generally unreactive' because their strong single covalent bonds resist many reactions, but they do react readily with oxygen in combustion, releasing energy; 'generally unreactive' is a comparison with more reactive families (such as the alkenes met in the next lesson), not a claim of total inertness.
misconceptions.remediation: Point directly at the combustion equation being studied in this lesson and ask the learner to reconcile it with the claim 'alkanes never react'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel mainly produces carbon monoxide, CO.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Carbon monoxide is widely discussed as a dangerous combustion product, so learners sometimes assume it is the main or even the only product, rather than a product of incomplete combustion specifically.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes CO instead of CO2 as a product when asked to balance a complete combustion equation.
misconceptions.correct_model: Complete combustion, which happens when there is a plentiful supply of oxygen, produces carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) as the main products. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a product of incomplete combustion, when oxygen supply is limited; this lesson covers complete combustion only.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the general word statement 'hydrocarbon + oxygen (plentiful) -> carbon dioxide + water' and have the learner compare it directly against any equation they produce before checking atom balance.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing 'saturated' (bonding) with 'saturated solution' (dissolving).
common_mistakes.why: Both share the everyday sense of 'completely full', but they describe entirely different physical situations.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state which meaning is intended: bonding (single bonds only) or dissolving (maximum solute).

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating 'alkanes are unreactive' as an absolute rule with no exceptions.
common_mistakes.why: The word 'unreactive' sounds total, rather than comparative.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember combustion as the standing counter-example: alkanes do react with oxygen when ignited.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing CO instead of CO2 as a complete-combustion product.
common_mistakes.why: Carbon monoxide is a familiar, often-discussed substance, so it comes to mind before checking which combustion conditions (complete versus incomplete) actually produce it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the oxygen supply stated in the question: plentiful oxygen means complete combustion, which always gives CO2, never CO.

exam_notes: When balancing a hydrocarbon combustion equation, balance carbon first, hydrogen second, and oxygen last; double every coefficient if the oxygen total comes out odd.
State explicitly that combustion requires a plentiful oxygen supply when claiming CO2 (rather than CO) as the carbon-containing product.
'Generally unreactive' should be justified by bonding (strong single bonds), not simply asserted.

summary.big_idea: Alkanes' strong single covalent bonds make them generally unreactive, with complete combustion in plentiful oxygen, forming carbon dioxide and water, as the key exception.
key_points: Saturated means only single C-C bonds; this is unrelated to a saturated solution.
Strong single bonds explain why alkanes undergo relatively few reactions.
Complete combustion (plentiful oxygen) of any hydrocarbon fuel produces CO2 and H2O.
A combustion equation balances by fixing carbon, then hydrogen, then whatever oxygen total those require.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Alkanes are saturated (single bonds only) and generally unreactive, but burn readily in plentiful oxygen to give CO2 and H2O; balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen.

exit_check.question: A student claims propane cannot be a fuel because 'alkanes don't react'. Using one equation, show this claim is wrong.
exit_check.answer: Propane burns in plentiful oxygen: $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8} + 5O_{2} \to 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}$. This is a real reaction that releases energy, directly contradicting the claim that alkanes never react; 'generally unreactive' allows for combustion as the key exception.

theory_blocks.title: An open door the alkane doesn't have
theory_blocks.body:
An alkene's C=C double bond is, chemically, an open door that a saturated alkane simply does not have: one of the two shared electron pairs in the double bond can break open, letting the two carbons each form a new single bond to an incoming atom, without losing any carbon atoms from the chain.

This single structural feature, the C=C double bond, is the reason alkenes are far more reactive than alkanes and undergo a whole family of [[blue:**addition reactions**]] that alkanes cannot.

theory_blocks.title: The bromine-water test for unsaturation
theory_blocks.body:
Shaking a sample with orange **bromine water**: if the sample contains a C=C double bond, the bromine adds across it (forming a colourless dibromo-compound), and the bromine water's orange colour disappears.

If the sample is saturated (no C=C bond, such as an alkane), there is no double bond for the bromine to add across, and the bromine water stays orange.

This decolourisation is the standard chemical test for unsaturation, and it only gives a positive result because of the C=C bond specifically, not because the sample is 'organic' in general.

theory_blocks.title: Cracking: breaking a large alkane apart
theory_blocks.body:
Long-chain alkanes from the lower fractions (which are less useful and in lower demand) of crude oil can be broken down by **cracking**: heating the vapour to a high temperature in the presence of a catalyst, which breaks some C-C bonds in the long chain.

Cracking always produces at least one alkene, together with a smaller alkane or hydrogen: there are not enough hydrogen atoms to make every product saturated, so at least one product must contain a C=C double bond.

For example: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \to C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}}$ (decane cracks into octane and ethene), and $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6} \to C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2}}$ (ethane cracks into ethene and hydrogen).

Cracking is therefore used to manufacture both alkenes and hydrogen. This matters industrially because it converts less useful long-chain fractions into more useful shorter-chain alkanes and into alkenes,

which this lesson's remaining reactions depend on.

theory_blocks.title: Three named addition reactions
theory_blocks.body:
An alkene's C=C double bond can open to add each of three different reagents, with its own catalyst in each case:

- **Bromine**: alkene + $\mathrm{Br_{2}}$ $\to$ a dibromo-compound (no catalyst needed; this is the same reaction behind the bromine-water test).
- **Hydrogen**, using a **nickel (Ni)** catalyst (hydrogenation): alkene + $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ $\to$ the corresponding alkane. For example, ethene + hydrogen $\to$ ethane.
- **Steam**, using an **acid** catalyst: alkene + $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ $\to$ the corresponding alcohol. For example, ethene + steam $\to$ ethanol.

In every case, the double bond opens into a single bond and each carbon that was part of the C=C forms one new bond to an atom from the added reagent; the number of carbon atoms in the chain never changes during addition.
