objectives.statement: Distinguish condensation polymerisation from addition polymerisation by whether a small molecule is released, identify the amide linkage (-CO-NH-) in nylon, and describe or draw the repeat unit of a supplied nylon structure with its repeating boundary clearly marked.

prerequisites.statement: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening their C=C double bonds, with no small molecule released, and the repeat unit's atoms exactly match the monomer's.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Condensation polymerisation is best understood by contrast with addition polymerisation; without a firm grip on the addition case, the difference (a small molecule released, no double bond involved) has nothing to contrast against.

prerequisites.statement: A repeat unit is the smallest group of atoms that, repeated many times, reproduces a polymer's whole chain, usually marked with square brackets and a subscript n.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding nylon's repeat unit means applying exactly this same idea to a more complex, two-linkage structure.

diagnostic_items.question: Based on your prior knowledge: . What is the key concept here?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Student should demonstrate basic understanding of condensation polymers and nylon.
diagnostic_items.interpretation: If incorrect, review foundational concepts before proceeding with Condensation polymers and nylon.

theory_blocks.title: A different joining mechanism entirely
theory_blocks.body:
Not every polymer forms by opening a C=C double bond. **Condensation polymerisation** joins monomers by a reaction between suitable functional groups on each one, and, unlike addition polymerisation, it [[blue:**releases a small molecule**]] (commonly water) as each new link forms.

Nylon, a widely used polyamide, forms this way: its monomers contain no C=C double bond, and its chain contains nitrogen and oxygen atoms in amide linkages, rather than the all-carbon chain of an addition polymer.

assets.caption: Nylon forms by condensation: the -OH of each acid group and an H of each amine group (both red) leave as water, and the acid's carbon bonds straight to the nitrogen to make an amide linkage, -CO-NH-.
assets.purpose: Shows the condensation mechanism itself: nylon-6,6's two monomer types (a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine), the amide linkage formed, and the water released at each link.

theory_blocks.title: The amide linkage in nylon
theory_blocks.body:
Nylon's chain repeatedly contains an **amide linkage**, $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$: a carbon (double-bonded to oxygen) bonded to a nitrogen (also bonded to one hydrogen).

In the widely used nylon-6,6, each repeat unit contains **two** amide linkages, joining a six-carbon chain segment to a four-carbon chain segment: $[-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-]_n$.

Every nitrogen in this structure forms three bonds (to hydrogen, to a chain carbon, and to a carbonyl carbon); every carbonyl carbon forms four bonds (a double bond to oxygen, plus two single bonds, one to nitrogen and one to the chain).

Nylon-6,6's chain is built from **two different monomers**, each carrying two reactive groups: a **dicarboxylic acid**, $\mathrm{HOOC}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{COOH}$, and a **diamine**, $\mathrm{H_2N}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH_2}$.

Wherever a $-\mathrm{COOH}$ group meets an $-\mathrm{NH_2}$ group, an amide linkage forms and a molecule of water is released: $-\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{H_2N}- \rightarrow -\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}- + \mathrm{H_2O}$.

Because each repeat unit contains two amide linkages, **two** molecules of water are released for every repeat unit added to the chain, and because every monomer has a reactive group at each end the chain can keep growing from both ends.

assets.caption: The repeat unit of nylon-6,6: two amide linkages (-CO-NH-) joined by six-carbon and four-carbon chain segments, with the repeat-unit boundary marked by brackets and open bonds crossing them to show the chain continues.
assets.purpose: Lets a learner locate both amide linkages and verify the repeat-unit boundary reproduces the chain, directly addressing declared gap DISC-C11-02.

theory_blocks.title: Finding a valid repeat-unit boundary
theory_blocks.body:
To mark a repeat unit correctly on any polymer chain: find a recognisable, repeating feature (here, an amide linkage), decide on a cut point just before or after it, make the identical cut at the equivalent point one repeat further along the chain, and check that the atoms between the two cuts, repeated end to end, reproduce the real chain exactly, with every bond continuing correctly across each boundary.

Where the first cut goes is a free choice (for nylon-6,6 the brackets are usually drawn across the C-N bond of an amide linkage, as in the diagram above), provided the second cut is at the equivalent point exactly one repeat further along.

A boundary is invalid if the stretch between the cuts is not exactly one repeat, for example if it leaves out an $-\mathrm{NH}-$ or a $-\mathrm{CO}-$ group, because copies placed end to end would then not rebuild the real chain.

theory_blocks.title: Addition and condensation, side by side
theory_blocks.body:
- **Addition polymerisation** (poly(ethene), previous lesson): monomer has a C=C double bond, which opens; no small molecule is released; repeat unit's atoms exactly match one monomer's atoms.
- **Condensation polymerisation** (nylon, this lesson): monomers react at suitable functional groups (no C=C bond involved); a small molecule (commonly water) is released at each new link; the repeat unit's atoms do **not** simply match one starting monomer's atoms, because some atoms have left as the released small molecule.

To decide from a structure which mechanism produced a polymer, look at the main chain: if it is made only of carbon atoms (each repeat unit built from the two carbons of an opened C=C bond, with any other atoms hanging off them), it is an addition polymer;

if the chain contains linkages such as the amide linkage $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$, it is a condensation polymer. Looking for a C=C double bond does not work: neither type has one left in its repeat unit.

keywords.definition: Polymerisation in which monomers join by reaction at functional groups, releasing a small molecule (commonly water) at each new link.
The repeating structural feature -CO-NH- found in a polyamide such as nylon, where a carbonyl carbon bonds directly to a nitrogen.
A polymer whose repeat unit contains amide linkages, such as nylon.
A molecule with an amine group, -NH2, at each end; one of the two monomers that make nylon.
A molecule with a carboxylic acid group, -COOH, at each end; the other monomer that makes nylon.

worked_examples.statement: **Spotting the mechanism.** A polymer's repeat unit is examined and found to contain no C=C double bond anywhere, but does contain a repeating $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$ linkage. State which type of polymerisation most likely produced this polymer, and justify your answer.
worked_examples.solution:
- The absence of a C=C double bond does not decide the question on its own: addition polymers such as poly(ethene) also have no C=C left in their repeat units, because the double bond opens during polymerisation.
- The deciding feature is the repeating $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$ (amide) linkage in the chain. An addition polymer's main chain is made only of carbon atoms; an amide linkage, containing nitrogen and oxygen, forms when two functional groups react together and release a small molecule (water).
- This polymer is a polyamide, so it was most likely produced by condensation polymerisation.
worked_examples.interpretation: The evidence is the amide linkage in the chain, not the missing C=C bond: every addition polymer also lacks a C=C bond in its repeat unit.

worked_examples.statement: **Locating the amide linkages.** In the nylon-6,6 repeat unit, $-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-$, identify both amide linkages and state what separates them.
worked_examples.solution:
- An amide linkage has the pattern $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$ (or equivalently $-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-$ read the other way): a carbonyl carbon directly bonded to an amide nitrogen.
- The first amide linkage sits between the end of the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$ segment and the start of the $\mathrm{CO}$ that begins the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ segment, read across the $-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-$ in the middle of the unit.
- The second amide linkage sits at the repeat-unit boundary itself, where this unit's final $-\mathrm{CO}-$ joins the next unit's opening $-\mathrm{NH}-$ (crossing the bracket).
- The two amide linkages are separated by the six-carbon $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$ segment on one side and the four-carbon $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ segment on the other. (The name nylon-6,6 comes from the six carbon atoms in each monomer: the diamine's $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$, and the diacid's $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ plus its two C=O carbons.)
worked_examples.interpretation: Locating both linkages, including the one that crosses the bracket into the next repeat, is what confirms the boundary has been drawn correctly.

worked_examples.statement: **Checking a proposed repeat unit.** A student proposes the repeat unit of nylon-6,6 as $-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-$. Explain why this is not a valid repeat unit, and give a correct one.
worked_examples.solution:
- Place two copies of the student's unit end to end: the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ at the end of one copy joins directly to the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$ at the start of the next, giving a run of ten $\mathrm{CH_{2}}$ groups with no amide linkage between them, which never occurs in real nylon-6,6.
- The reason is that the unit is not one complete repeat: compared with the true repeat unit $-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-$, it is missing one $-\mathrm{NH}-$ group and one $-\mathrm{CO}-$ group, so it contains only one amide linkage per unit instead of two ($\mathrm{C_{11}H_{21}NO}$ instead of $\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}N_{2}O_{2}}$).
- A correct repeat unit makes identical cuts exactly one repeat apart, for example $-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-$ (brackets across the C-N bond of an amide linkage, as in the lesson's diagram) or, equally valid, $-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-$.
- The test is always the same: copies placed end to end must rebuild the real chain atom for atom and bond for bond.
worked_examples.interpretation: This targets the idea that any stretch of chain that 'looks like' nylon is a repeat unit; the test is whether repeated copies rebuild the real chain, which also means the unit must contain exactly one repeat's worth of atoms.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Accepting a proposed unit because it contains an amide linkage and both CH2 segments, without placing two copies end to end to check that the real chain is rebuilt.

guided_exercises.statement: State one structural feature you could look for to decide whether an unfamiliar polymer was most likely made by addition or by condensation polymerisation, and explain your reasoning.
hints: Think about what an addition polymer's main chain is made of: which atoms come from the opened C=C double bonds of the alkene monomers?
Does a condensation polymer such as nylon have only carbon atoms in its main chain, or does it contain a linkage with other atoms in it?
guided_exercises.answer: Look at the main chain of the repeat unit. In an addition polymer the main chain is made only of carbon atoms (from the opened C=C bonds of the alkene monomer), and the repeat unit has exactly the same atoms as one monomer. In a condensation polymer the chain contains linkages such as the amide linkage $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$, with nitrogen and oxygen atoms in the chain, formed when functional groups react and release a small molecule. (Looking for a C=C double bond does not work: neither type has one left in its repeat unit.)
common_errors: Looking only for the presence of carbon and hydrogen (present in both mechanisms' products) rather than specifically for a C=C double bond or a repeating linkage such as -CO-NH-.

guided_exercises.statement: State what distinguishes condensation polymerisation from addition polymerisation in terms of what is released during the reaction.
hints: Does addition polymerisation release anything besides the polymer itself?
What is commonly released during condensation polymerisation?
guided_exercises.answer: Addition polymerisation releases nothing: every atom in the monomers ends up in the polymer. Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (commonly water) as each new link between monomers forms, so the polymer's repeat unit does not contain every atom that was originally present in the separate monomers.
common_errors: Assuming condensation polymerisation, like addition polymerisation, releases nothing, since both processes are collectively called 'polymerisation'.

exercises.statement: State two differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
exercises.answer: (1) Addition polymerisation requires a C=C double bond in the monomer, which opens during the reaction; condensation polymerisation involves no C=C double bond, joining monomers at other functional groups instead. (2) Addition polymerisation releases no small molecule, so the repeat unit's atoms exactly match the monomer's; condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (commonly water) at each new link, so the repeat unit does not contain every atom originally present in the separate monomers.

exercises.statement: Write the general structure of an amide linkage, and state which two types of atom are directly bonded to each other within it.
exercises.answer: The amide linkage is $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$. The carbon of the carbonyl group ($\mathrm{C}{=}\mathrm{O}$) is directly bonded to the nitrogen atom.

exercises.statement: Explain why the repeat unit of nylon-6,6 must contain two -NH- groups and two -CO- groups, and why it does not matter at which point along the chain the first bracket is drawn.
exercises.answer: A repeat unit must be exactly one repeat of the chain. Nylon-6,6's chain repeats the sequence $-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-$, which contains two $-\mathrm{NH}-$ and two $-\mathrm{CO}-$ groups; a shorter stretch would leave some of these out, so copies placed end to end would not rebuild the real chain. Where the first bracket goes is a free choice, because the second bracket is drawn at the equivalent point exactly one repeat further along: whatever the starting point, the unit contains the same atoms in the same order, just starting at a different place.

exercises.statement: A different polyamide's repeat unit is described as containing one $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$ linkage per repeat unit, rather than nylon-6,6's two. Using the reasoning developed in this lesson (not any new fact), state whether this polymer was most likely formed by addition or by condensation polymerisation, and justify your answer.
exercises.answer: This polymer was most likely formed by condensation polymerisation. The presence of an amide linkage, $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$, is the structural signature used throughout this lesson to identify polyamides formed by monomers joining with release of a small molecule; a C=C double bond, the signature of addition polymerisation, plays no role in forming or describing an amide linkage. The number of amide linkages per repeat unit (one here, versus two in nylon-6,6) affects the specific chain pattern, not which general mechanism (addition or condensation) was responsible.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Condensation polymers and nylon'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Condensation polymers and nylon' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Condensation polymers and nylon' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: (a) State one key difference between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. (b) Name the type of linkage found repeatedly in nylon's structure, and write its general form.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Addition polymerisation releases no small molecule and requires a C=C double bond that opens; condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (commonly water) and does not require a C=C double bond. (b) The amide linkage, $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$.
mark_scheme: States a correct difference involving release (or not) of a small molecule.
Correctly links addition polymerisation to a C=C double bond opening.
Names the amide linkage.
Gives the correct general form -CO-NH- (or equivalent -NH-CO-).

exam_questions.statement: The repeat unit of nylon-6,6 is $[-\mathrm{NH}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4-\mathrm{CO}-]_n$. (a) Identify both amide linkages in this repeat unit. (b) Explain, using this structure, why nylon cannot have formed by addition polymerisation. (c) State what a valid repeat-unit boundary must do when it is drawn across a linkage such as this one.
exam_questions.answer: (a) One amide linkage is within the unit, between the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$ segment and the $\mathrm{CO}$ that starts the $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ segment (reading $-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-$); the second is at the bracket boundary itself, where this unit's closing $-\mathrm{CO}-$ connects to the next unit's opening $-\mathrm{NH}-$. (b) The chain contains amide linkages, $-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-$, so nitrogen and oxygen atoms are part of the main chain. An addition polymer's main chain is made only of carbon atoms (from opened C=C bonds), and its repeat unit has the same atoms as one alkene monomer; amide linkages can only form when functional groups react with the loss of a small molecule (water), so nylon is a condensation polymer. (c) The two brackets must cut the chain at equivalent points exactly one repeat apart (here, across the C-N bond of an amide linkage, so that this unit's $-\mathrm{CO}-$ bonds to the next unit's $-\mathrm{NH}-$), so that repeating the unit reconstructs the real chain.
mark_scheme: Correctly identifies the internal amide linkage.
Correctly identifies the boundary-crossing amide linkage.
States the chain contains amide linkages, with N and O atoms in the main chain.
States that an addition polymer's main chain contains only carbon atoms / amide linkages form only by condensation with loss of water, so nylon is not an addition polymer.
States the brackets cut the chain at equivalent points exactly one repeat apart (here across an amide C-N bond).
Explains this ensures repeated copies reconstruct the real chain.

challenge_questions.statement: A student argues: 'nylon must actually be an addition polymer, because the -CO-NH- amide linkage is just an open bond crossing a bracket, exactly like poly(ethene)'s repeat unit has open bonds crossing its brackets.' Evaluate this argument, distinguishing what is genuinely similar between the two cases from what is different.
hints: Both repeat units do have bonds crossing their brackets; what specifically do those crossing bonds represent in each case?
In poly(ethene), where did the crossing bonds originally come from, before polymerisation?
challenge_questions.answer: The student is right that both repeat units show bonds crossing their brackets, representing the chain's continuation, but this surface similarity does not make the two mechanisms the same. In poly(ethene), the crossing bonds are new C-C bonds formed when each monomer's C=C double bond opened during addition polymerisation; no atoms were lost, and the repeat unit's formula exactly matches the monomer's. In nylon, the bond crossing the bracket at the amide boundary is a C-N single bond formed when two different monomers (a diamine and a diacid) reacted together with the loss of a small molecule (water); there was no double bond opening, and the repeat unit's atoms do not match a single starting monomer's atoms, because some atoms left as the released water. The argument confuses 'a bond crosses the bracket' (true of any repeat unit, addition or condensation) with 'the bond came from an opened C=C double bond' (true only for addition polymerisation), so the conclusion that nylon must be an addition polymer does not follow.
common_errors: Treating 'bonds cross the repeat-unit bracket' as a feature unique to addition polymerisation, when in fact every repeat unit, regardless of mechanism, must show its chain continuing somehow.

challenge_questions.statement:
Nylon is a condensation polymer.
(a) Explain the difference between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. (3 marks)
(b) State what small molecule is released during condensation polymerisation. (1 mark)
(c) Nylon has many uses. Give two properties of nylon and explain how each makes it suitable for making rope. (2 marks)
(d) Suggest why condensation polymers are generally easier to recycle than addition polymers. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) In addition polymerisation, unsaturated monomers (with C=C bonds) join together, and no other molecule is produced. In condensation polymerisation, two different monomers with functional groups at each end react, and a small molecule (usually water) is eliminated with each link formed.
(b) Water (H₂O).
(c) (1) Nylon is strong/tough — it can withstand high tension forces without breaking. (2) Nylon is resistant to abrasion/wear — it lasts a long time even with friction.
(d) Condensation polymers can be broken down (hydrolysed) back into their monomers by heating with acid or alkali, because the links between monomers are susceptible to hydrolysis. Addition polymers have only strong C—C bonds along the backbone, which are much harder to break.

mcq.stem: What is released during condensation polymerisation that is not released during addition polymerisation?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas
options.why_wrong: the small molecule typically released in condensation polymerisation (such as nylon's formation) is water, not carbon dioxide.

options.text: Hydrogen gas
options.why_wrong: hydrogen gas is not the small molecule released during condensation polymerisation; water is the molecule commonly released.

options.text: A small molecule, commonly water.
Nothing; both mechanisms release the same products.
options.why_wrong: this is backwards; addition polymerisation releases nothing, while condensation polymerisation specifically releases a small molecule, which is exactly what distinguishes the two mechanisms.

mcq.explanation: Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule, commonly water, at each new link; addition polymerisation releases nothing.

mcq.stem: What structural feature in a repeat unit would rule out addition polymerisation as the method used to form that polymer?

options.text: The presence of carbon atoms.
options.why_wrong: both addition and condensation polymers contain carbon atoms; this is not a distinguishing feature.

options.text: The presence of hydrogen atoms.
options.why_wrong: both addition and condensation polymers typically contain hydrogen atoms; this is not a distinguishing feature.

options.text: A repeat unit drawn inside square brackets.
options.why_wrong: both addition and condensation polymers' repeat units are conventionally drawn inside square brackets with a subscript n; this notation alone does not distinguish the mechanisms.

options.text: A linkage such as -CO-NH- in the main chain, containing atoms other than carbon.

mcq.explanation: An addition polymer's main chain is made only of carbon atoms from opened C=C bonds (and, like every polymer, has no C=C left in its repeat unit). A linkage such as -CO-NH- in the chain can only form by condensation, with a small molecule released, so it rules out addition polymerisation.

mcq.stem: In nylon's amide linkage, -CO-NH-, which two atoms are directly bonded to each other?

options.text: The carbonyl carbon and the nitrogen.
The carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen.
options.why_wrong: the oxygen is double-bonded to the carbon, not directly bonded to the nitrogen; the defining bond of the amide linkage is between the carbon and the nitrogen.

options.text: Two nitrogen atoms.
options.why_wrong: there is only one nitrogen in a single amide linkage; the linkage does not connect two nitrogens directly.

options.text: Two carbon atoms.
options.why_wrong: the amide linkage's key feature is specifically the carbon-nitrogen bond, not a carbon-carbon bond.

mcq.explanation: In the amide linkage -CO-NH-, the carbonyl carbon (double-bonded to oxygen) is directly, singly bonded to the amide nitrogen.

mcq.stem: A student draws a 'repeat unit' for nylon-6,6. When copies of it are placed end to end, a $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_4$ segment joins directly onto a $(\mathrm{CH_{2}})_6$ segment with no amide linkage between them. Why is this repeat unit not valid?

options.text: Because a repeat unit must always start with a nitrogen atom.
options.why_wrong: a repeat unit can start at any point along the chain, provided the second bracket is drawn at the equivalent point exactly one repeat further along; there is no rule about which atom comes first.

options.text: Because repeating that unit would not correctly reconstruct the real chain's bonding pattern.
Because amide linkages are not allowed to appear in a repeat unit at all.
options.why_wrong: amide linkages must appear in a nylon repeat unit; the issue is where the boundary is drawn relative to the linkage, not whether the linkage can appear.

options.text: Because square brackets cannot be placed next to a nitrogen atom.
options.why_wrong: there is no such restriction; the bracket's position is judged by whether the resulting repeat correctly reconstructs the chain, not by which atom happens to sit near it.

mcq.explanation: A valid repeat unit must reproduce the real chain exactly when copies are placed end to end. This unit leaves out part of one repeat (an -NH- and a -CO- group), so repeated copies join CH2 segments directly and do not rebuild nylon's chain.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes condensation polymerisation from addition polymerisation?
flashcards.back: Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (commonly water) as monomers join; addition polymerisation releases nothing.

flashcards.front: What is the general form of the amide linkage found in nylon?
flashcards.back: -CO-NH- (a carbonyl carbon bonded directly to an amide nitrogen).

flashcards.front: How does nylon's repeat unit differ from poly(ethene)'s in terms of what mechanism formed it?
flashcards.back: Poly(ethene) forms by addition polymerisation (C=C opens, no molecule released); nylon forms by condensation polymerisation (amide linkages form, water released, no C=C involved).

flashcards.front: Does every polymer form by a C=C double bond opening, the way poly(ethene) does?
flashcards.back: No. Condensation polymers such as nylon form by a completely different mechanism, joining monomers at functional groups and releasing a small molecule, with no C=C bond involved.

flashcards.front: How many amide linkages does one repeat unit of nylon-6,6 contain, and what separates them?
flashcards.back: Two amide linkages, separated by a six-carbon segment on one side and a four-carbon segment on the other.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Nylon, like poly(ethene), forms by opening a C=C double bond in its starting molecules.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Addition polymerisation (the only polymerisation mechanism met so far) is generalised to all polymers, including nylon, without checking whether nylon's monomers even contain a C=C bond.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes nylon's formation using 'the double bond opens' language, or looks for a C=C bond in nylon's repeat unit.
misconceptions.correct_model: Nylon forms by condensation polymerisation, a completely different mechanism from addition polymerisation: suitable functional groups on two different monomers react together, releasing a small molecule, with no C=C double bond involved at any stage.
misconceptions.remediation: Show the learner nylon's two monomers (a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid) and ask them to find a C=C double bond in either; finding none, and seeing that water is released as each amide linkage forms, shows that a different mechanism, not addition, must be responsible.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any stretch of a polymer chain that contains the right-looking groups can be used as the repeat unit; the two ends do not need to be exactly one repeat apart.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Having only met one simple repeat unit before (poly(ethene)'s, with an obvious symmetric boundary), learners have not yet needed to think carefully about where a less obvious boundary must fall.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a 'repeat unit' for nylon that, when repeated, does not reproduce the continuing chain (for example, it leaves out an -NH- or a -CO- group, so CH2 segments end up joined directly).
misconceptions.correct_model: The first bracket can go at any point along the chain, but the second must be drawn at the equivalent point exactly one repeat further along, so that repeating the unit end to end reproduces the real chain atom for atom. For nylon-6,6 every correct repeat unit contains two -NH- groups, two -CO- groups, a (CH2)6 segment and a (CH2)4 segment (C12H22N2O2), whichever starting point is chosen.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the learner draw two full repeats of their proposed unit side by side and check, bond by bond, whether the joined structure matches a genuine continuing nylon chain.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Condensation polymerisation, like addition polymerisation, releases no small molecule; 'condensation' here just means 'a different starting material'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'condensation' is not everyday chemistry vocabulary for most learners, so without a clear definition it is sometimes treated as a synonym for 'another kind of addition'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states nylon's formation releases nothing, or cannot name what small molecule is released during condensation polymerisation.
misconceptions.correct_model: Condensation polymerisation specifically releases a small molecule (commonly water) as the monomers join; this is the opposite of addition polymerisation, which releases nothing. 'Condensation' describes this small-molecule-releasing mechanism, not simply 'a different starting material'.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast the two polymerisation types side by side in a table (mechanism, bond involved, small molecule released or not) and have the learner fill every cell.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing nylon's formation using 'the double bond opens' language borrowed from addition polymerisation.
common_mistakes.why: Addition polymerisation was the only mechanism met before this lesson, so its language generalises by habit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the monomers: nylon's monomers have no C=C double bond, so 'the double bond opens' cannot describe its formation; point to the amide linkages formed (with water released) instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing a 'repeat unit' for nylon that is not exactly one repeat long (for example, leaving out an -NH- or a -CO- group).
common_mistakes.why: Only one simple, symmetric repeat-unit boundary (poly(ethene)'s) had been met before, so the need to check a boundary carefully was not yet practised.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check that repeating the proposed unit end to end reconstructs the real chain's bonding pattern, not just that the atom count looks reasonable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming condensation polymerisation, like addition polymerisation, releases nothing.
common_mistakes.why: Both processes share the word 'polymerisation', inviting the assumption that they behave identically in every respect.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the small molecule released (commonly water) whenever describing condensation polymerisation, to keep the contrast with addition explicit.

exam_notes: State explicitly whether a small molecule is released (and name it, usually water) when describing or comparing polymerisation mechanisms.

To judge from a structure whether a polymer is an addition or a condensation polymer, look at the main chain: only carbon atoms means addition; linkages such as -CO-NH- mean condensation. Neither type has a C=C double bond left in its repeat unit.
When asked to validate a proposed repeat unit, check that repeating it reconstructs the real chain's bonding, not just that its atom count looks plausible.

summary.big_idea: Condensation polymerisation, unlike addition polymerisation, joins monomers at functional groups with no C=C bond involved and releases a small molecule, which is exactly how nylon's amide-linked repeat unit forms.
key_points: Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (commonly water); addition polymerisation releases nothing.
The amide linkage, -CO-NH-, is nylon's repeating structural signature, with no C=C double bond involved anywhere.
Nylon-6,6's repeat unit contains two amide linkages separated by six-carbon and four-carbon segments.
A valid repeat-unit boundary must reconstruct the real chain's bonding exactly when repeated, not merely contain a plausible atom count.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A repeating -CO-NH- linkage in the chain, formed with water released, means condensation polymerisation (not addition); a valid repeat unit must rebuild the real chain when repeated, not just look right.

exit_check.question: A student insists nylon must contain a C=C double bond somewhere, 'because all polymers come from double bonds opening up.' How would you use nylon's own repeat unit to correct this?
exit_check.answer: Point to the amide linkages, -CO-NH-, in nylon's repeat unit: they put nitrogen and oxygen atoms into the main chain, which opening C=C double bonds could never do (an addition polymer's chain is made only of carbon atoms). These linkages form when the functional groups of two different monomers, neither containing a C=C bond, react together and release water: the signature of condensation polymerisation, a completely different mechanism from the C=C-opening addition polymerisation the student is generalising from.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from organic chemistry accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Why is the sulfur content of fuels a problem with the fuels we use?
exercises.answer: Sulfur impurities in fuels burn to form sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.
exercises.full_solution: Natural gas and other fossil fuels are mixtures of hydrocarbons but may also contain small amounts of sulfur compounds. When the fuel is burned, this sulfur is oxidised along with the hydrocarbon, forming sulfur dioxide gas (S + O2 -> SO2). Sulfur dioxide released into the atmosphere dissolves in water droplets in clouds and is further oxidised, forming sulfurous and sulfuric acid. This falls as acid rain, which damages trees and vegetation, acidifies lakes and rivers (harming aquatic life), and erodes stone buildings and statues (especially those made of limestone/marble). It can also contribute to respiratory problems in humans. This is why fuel suppliers try to use low-sulfur fuels (some natural gas, such as North Sea gas, is naturally low in sulfur) or remove sulfur before combustion.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: The combustion of methane (natural gas) is an oxidation reaction. Explain with respect to this reaction the term oxidation.
exercises.answer: Oxidation here means the carbon and hydrogen atoms in methane gain oxygen (are combined with oxygen) as they are converted into carbon dioxide and water.
exercises.full_solution: The combustion reaction is CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l) (atom-balance check: left side C1 H4 O4; right side C1 O2+2=4, H4 -- balanced). In this reaction, oxidation is defined as the gain of oxygen by a substance. The carbon atom in methane (bonded only to hydrogen) ends up bonded to oxygen in carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen atoms end up bonded to oxygen in water. Both the carbon and the hydrogen in methane have therefore gained oxygen, so methane has been oxidised. (Oxygen itself is the oxidising agent, and it is reduced/consumed in the process, but the question asks specifically about oxidation of the fuel.)

exercises.statement: Estimate the boiling points for the alkanes with formulae: (a) $C_7H_{16}$ (b) $C_8H_{18}$.
exercises.answer: (a) $C_7H_{16}$ (heptane): approximately 95-100 °C. (b) $C_8H_{18}$ (octane): approximately 120-130 °C.
exercises.full_solution: The boiling points of the first four alkanes are: methane (n = 1) −162 °C, ethane (n = 2) −89 °C, propane (n = 3) −42 °C, butane (n = 4) 0 °C. To estimate the boiling points of later members, plot boiling point against the number of carbon atoms (n) and extend (extrapolate) the smooth curve. The increase for each extra CH2 group is +73, +47 and +42 °C for the first three steps: the curve rises steeply at first and then becomes gradually less steep. If the curve is continued with rises of roughly +35 to +30 °C per extra carbon atom, it gives about 35 °C for pentane (n = 5), about 68 °C for hexane (n = 6), about 98 °C for heptane (n = 7) and about 126 °C for octane (n = 8). Any sensible extrapolation is acceptable (heptane roughly 90-105 °C, octane roughly 115-135 °C); the actual values are 98 °C for heptane and 126 °C for octane. The boiling points rise because the intermolecular forces get stronger as the molecules get bigger.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Name the alkanes which have the following formulae: (a) $C_7H_{16}$ (b) $C_{10}H_{22}$.
exercises.answer: (a) Heptane. (b) Decane.
exercises.full_solution: Both formulae fit the alkane general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$: for (a) n=7 gives $2(7)+2=16$ hydrogens, matching $C_7H_{16}$, and the alkane prefix for 7 carbons is 'hept-', so the name is heptane. For (b) n=10 gives $2(10)+2=22$ hydrogens, matching $C_{10}H_{22}$, and the prefix for 10 carbons is 'dec-', so the name is decane.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: What is meant by the term 'addition reaction'?
exercises.answer: An addition reaction is one in which two (or more) molecules combine to form a single larger molecule, with no other product formed, usually by one of the two bonds of a C=C double bond breaking so that extra atoms can join the molecule.
exercises.full_solution: Alkenes are unsaturated because they contain a C=C double bond. One of the two bonds making up this double bond can break, freeing up a bonding position on each carbon atom. Other atoms (such as Br, Cl, H) can then bond to these positions. Because the whole of both reacting molecules ends up in a single product molecule (e.g. ethene + bromine -> dibromoethane, with nothing else produced), this type of reaction is called addition: the atoms of the small molecule are simply 'added across' the double bond.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Write a word and balanced chemical equation for the reaction between ethene and hydrogen chloride.
exercises.answer: Word equation: ethene + hydrogen chloride -> chloroethane. Balanced equation: $C_2H_4(g) + HCl(g) \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl(g)$
exercises.full_solution: This is an addition reaction across the C=C double bond of ethene, the same pattern as the addition of bromine or of steam to ethene. The H-Cl bond breaks, with H adding to one carbon and Cl adding to the other, giving chloroethane: $C_2H_4(g) + HCl(g) \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl(g)$. Atom check: left side has C2 H5 Cl1 (4 H from ethene + 1 H from HCl = 5), right side C2H5Cl has C2 H5 Cl1 -- balanced, and already has a 1:1:1 ratio so no further balancing coefficients are needed.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Write the structural formula for pentene.
exercises.answer: $CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$ (pent-1-ene), molecular formula $C_5H_{10}$.
exercises.full_solution: Pentene is the 5-carbon member of the alkene homologous series, general formula $C_nH_{2n}$, so for n=5 the molecular formula is $C_5H_{10}$. Drawing a straight chain of 5 carbons with one C=C double bond (placed at the end of the chain, since no locant is specified, the simplest/default answer is pent-1-ene) gives: $CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$. Checking the hydrogen count: the two double-bond carbons carry 2 H and 1 H respectively, the next two CH2 carbons carry 2 H each, and the terminal carbon carries 3 H, giving 2+1+2+2+3 = 10 H total, matching $C_5H_{10}$.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Which of the following organic chemicals are alkanes or alkenes? Propene, $C_3H_6$; Butanol, $C_4H_9OH$; Octane, $C_8H_{18}$; Nonane, $C_9H_{20}$; Methanoic acid, $HCOOH$; Butene, $C_4H_8$. State why you have chosen your answers.
exercises.answer: Propene: alkene. Butanol: neither (it is an alcohol). Octane: alkane. Nonane: alkane. Methanoic acid: neither (it is a carboxylic acid). Butene: alkene.
exercises.full_solution: Check each formula against the alkane general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$ and the alkene general formula $C_nH_{2n}$: Propene $C_3H_6$ has n=3, and $2n=6$ matches, so it is an alkene (and it already has the '-ene' ending). Octane $C_8H_{18}$ has n=8, and $2n+2=18$ matches, so it is an alkane ('-ane' ending). Nonane $C_9H_{20}$ has n=9, and $2n+2=20$ matches, so it is also an alkane. Butene $C_4H_8$ has n=4, and $2n=8$ matches, so it is an alkene. Butanol $C_4H_9OH$ fits the alcohol general formula $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$ (n=4 gives $2n+1=9$ H on the carbon skeleton) -- its '-ol' ending and the O-H group confirm it is an alcohol, not an alkane or alkene. Methanoic acid $HCOOH$ (overall formula $CH_2O_2$) fits the carboxylic acid general formula $C_nH_{2n}O_2$ (n=1 gives $2n=2$) -- its '-oic acid' name and COOH group confirm it is a carboxylic acid, not an alkane or alkene.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Explain why alcoholic drinks go sour if left open to the atmosphere for some time.
exercises.answer: The ethanol in the drink is slowly oxidised by oxygen in the air to ethanoic acid (vinegar), which has a sour/sharp taste.
exercises.full_solution: Ethanol, the alcohol present in drinks such as wine, reacts with oxygen from the air over time (this oxidation can also be helped along by naturally present acetic acid bacteria). The ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, $CH_3CH_2OH + O_2 \rightarrow CH_3COOH + H_2O$. Ethanoic acid is the acid found in vinegar, and it has a sharp, sour taste and smell, which is why an open bottle of wine left exposed to air for a while tastes sour/'has gone off'.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)
exercises.source_label: Chapter C14 'Formation of ethanol' Questions, Q9

exercises.statement: The equation below represents the fermentation process: $A \rightarrow B$ + carbon dioxide. (a) Identify and give the formulae of substances A and B. (b) Give a chemical test to identify carbon dioxide. (c) Which separation technique would you use to separate substance B from the fermentation mixture?
exercises.answer: (a) A is glucose, $C_6H_{12}O_6$; B is ethanol, $C_2H_5OH$. (b) Bubble the gas through limewater; if carbon dioxide is present the limewater turns milky/cloudy. (c) Fractional distillation.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The fermentation reaction is $C_6H_{12}O_6(aq) \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH(l) + 2CO_2(g)$, catalysed by yeast enzymes. Matching this to the general equation $A \rightarrow B$ + carbon dioxide, A (the starting material) is glucose, $C_6H_{12}O_6$, and B (the other product besides $CO_2$) is ethanol, $C_2H_5OH$ (atom check: left C6 H12 O6; right C 4 + 2 = 6, H 12, O 2 + 4 = 6 -- balanced). (b) The standard test for carbon dioxide gas is to bubble it through limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide); the limewater turns from colourless to a cloudy/milky white because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed. (c) The fermentation mixture is an aqueous solution containing ethanol (boiling point 78 °C), water (boiling point 100 °C) and dissolved solids/yeast. Because ethanol and water have different, fairly close boiling points, fractional distillation is used to separate and concentrate the ethanol from the rest of the mixture.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)
exercises.source_label: Chapter C14 'Formation of ethanol' Questions, Q10

exercises.statement: Write the general equation to represent the formation of polystyrene from its monomer.
exercises.answer: $n(CH_2=CH-C_6H_5) \rightarrow [-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)-]_n$
exercises.full_solution: Polystyrene is an addition polymer made from the monomer styrene (phenylethene), $CH_2=CH-C_6H_5$. In addition polymerisation, n molecules of the monomer join together by opening their C=C double bonds, with no other product formed, exactly as for poly(ethene) ($n(CH_2=CH_2) \rightarrow [-CH_2-CH_2-]_n$). Applying the same pattern to styrene: $n(CH_2=CH-C_6H_5) \rightarrow [-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)-]_n$. The repeating unit keeps every atom from the monomer (only the double bond has become a single bond), so the equation is automatically atom-balanced for any value of n.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Draw the structure of the repeating unit of the addition polymer formed from $CH_3-CH=CH_2$.
exercises.answer: Repeating unit: $[-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-]_n$, drawn as a carbon chain with alternating -CH(CH3)- and -CH2- groups (this is poly(propene)).
exercises.full_solution: $CH_3-CH=CH_2$ is propene. In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens, and each carbon forms a new single bond to the next monomer unit instead, while keeping its other substituents (the CH3 group and the H atoms) unchanged. So one carbon of the double bond keeps its CH3 group and one H (becoming -CH(CH3)-), and the other carbon keeps its two H atoms (becoming -CH2-). Linking many of these together gives the repeating unit $[-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-]_n$, drawn fully displayed as a zig-zag backbone of C-C bonds where every other carbon has a CH3 branch and an H above/below, and the carbons in between have two H atoms each.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Draw the structure of the monomer from which the addition polymer below has been produced. [The diagram shows three repeating units of the polymer chain, each unit consisting of a -CH(C6H5)- carbon bonded to a -CH2- carbon, i.e. the repeating pattern -CH(C6H5)-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2- with a C6H5 (phenyl) group and an H on every other backbone carbon, and two H atoms on each carbon in between.]
exercises.answer: $CH_2=CH-C_6H_5$ (styrene / phenylethene).
exercises.full_solution: Reading the drawn polymer chain, the repeating unit is $-CH(C_6H_5)-CH_2-$: one backbone carbon carries a phenyl group ($C_6H_5$) and one H, and the next backbone carbon carries two H atoms, and this pattern repeats. To find the monomer, reverse the polymerisation: since addition polymerisation simply opens a C=C double bond to join monomers with no atoms lost, the monomer must contain exactly the same atoms as one repeating unit, but joined by a double bond instead of two single bonds to neighbours. That gives $CH_2=CH-C_6H_5$ (styrene, systematic name phenylethene). The polymer shown is therefore polystyrene.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: A piece of cheese contains protein. Proteins are natural polymers made up of amino acids. There are 20 naturally occurring amino acids. The structures of two amino acids, glycine ($H_2N-CH_2-COOH$) and alanine ($H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH$), are shown. (a) Name the type of polymerisation involved in protein formation. (b) Draw a structural formula to represent the part of the protein chain formed by the reaction between the amino acids shown above.
exercises.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b) $H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH$ + $H_2O$ (a dipeptide formed by linking glycine to alanine through a peptide/amide bond, with a water molecule lost).
exercises.full_solution: (a) Proteins are formed when amino acid monomers join together, each time releasing a small molecule (water), which is the defining feature of condensation polymerisation (the same process that forms nylon). (b) Each amino acid has an -NH2 (amine) group at one end and a -COOH (carboxylic acid) group at the other. The -COOH of one amino acid reacts with the -NH2 of the next, releasing H2O and forming an amide (peptide) link, -CO-NH-. Taking the -COOH of glycine ($H_2N-CH_2-COOH$) and reacting it with the -NH2 of alanine ($H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH$) gives the dipeptide $H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH$, with a water molecule released. Atom check: glycine is $C_2H_5NO_2$ and alanine is $C_3H_7NO_2$; combined they give $C_5H_{12}N_2O_4$, and after losing one $H_2O$ the dipeptide is $C_5H_{10}N_2O_3$ -- both sides of glycine + alanine -> dipeptide + water balance exactly.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: (a) Name the polymerisation process that is used to make nylon. (b) Name the starting materials for: (i) nylon (ii) terylene. (c) Give the name and formula of the small molecule produced during the polymerisation reactions to produce nylon. (d) Give the name of the chemical link that holds together the nylon polymer chain. (e) Give two uses for nylon. (f) Explain the difference between the type of polymerisation you have named in part (a) and addition polymerisation.
exercises.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b)(i) 1,6-diaminohexane, $H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2$, and hexanedioic acid, $HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH$. (ii) Ethane-1,2-diol, $HO(CH_2)_2OH$, and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, $HOOC(C_6H_4)COOH$. (c) Water, $H_2O$. (d) The amide link (also called the peptide link). (e) Clothing/fabric (e.g. shirts, ties, parachutes) and ropes or racket strings (e.g. for tennis/badminton rackets). (f) Condensation polymerisation joins two different monomers, each losing a small molecule (water) at every new bond formed, so the product is not simply 'monomer repeated' and a second product (water) is formed; addition polymerisation uses a single type of unsaturated monomer that joins by opening its C=C double bond, with no other product formed and the polymer having the same empirical composition as the monomer.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Nylon is made from two different starting molecules that join with the loss of a water molecule at every new bond, so the process is condensation polymerisation. (b)(i) 1,6-diaminohexane, $H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2$, and hexanedioic acid, $HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH$. (ii) Ethane-1,2-diol, $HO(CH_2)_2OH$, and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, $HOOC(C_6H_4)COOH$. (c) Water, $H_2O$. One molecule is eliminated each time a diamine molecule and a diacid molecule react: $H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow H_2N(CH_2)_6NHOC(CH_2)_4COOH + H_2O$ (atom check: C12 H26 N2 O4 on both sides). (d) The amide link, -CO-NH- (the same link is called the peptide link in proteins). (e) Any two uses of nylon fibre, for example clothing such as shirts and ties, parachutes, ropes, or racket strings for tennis and badminton. (f) Condensation polymerisation uses two different monomers, each with a reactive group at both ends, and releases a small molecule (water) at every link, so the polymer's formula is the sum of the monomers' formulae minus one water molecule for each linkage. Addition polymerisation uses a single unsaturated monomer, which bonds to its neighbours by opening its C=C double bond; nothing else is produced, so the repeat unit contains exactly the same atoms as one monomer.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Explain the differences between an addition polymer and a condensation polymer.
exercises.answer: An addition polymer forms from a single type of unsaturated (C=C containing) monomer joining by opening the double bond, with no other product formed and the same empirical formula as the monomer. A condensation polymer usually forms from two different monomers (each with two reactive functional groups), joined by eliminating a small molecule such as water at every new bond.
exercises.full_solution: Addition polymerisation: only one kind of monomer is used, and it must be unsaturated (contain a C=C double bond), e.g. ethene forming poly(ethene) or styrene forming polystyrene. The double bond opens so each monomer can bond to its neighbours on both sides; nothing else is produced, so the repeating unit of the polymer has exactly the same atoms as the monomer, and the whole polymer chain can be written $-A-A-A-A-A-$, where A is the monomer unit. Condensation polymerisation: typically two different monomers are used (e.g. a diamine and a diacid for nylon, or a diol and a diacid for Terylene), each monomer having two reactive end groups so it can link to a monomer on each side. Every time a new bond (e.g. the amide link in nylon or the ester link in Terylene) forms between two monomers, a small molecule -- water in both of these examples -- is eliminated as a second product. The chain has the form $-A-B-A-B-A-B-$, and the polymer's formula is not simply 'monomer repeated': it is the sum of the two monomers' formulae minus one water molecule for every linkage formed.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)
